item.title: UBS: new banking rules, the Commission's compromise
item.description: 31 August 2026: CET-S approves stricter rules on foreign holdings of large banks, with 50% coverage in AT1 instead of 100% as proposed by the Federal Council.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The Economic Affairs Committee of the Council of States approves stricter rules for systemic banks (primarily UBS) - Compromise: 50% coverage with CET-1 own funds + 50% with AT1 bonds - Vote: 10 in favour, 2 against; the decision is not 'a gift to UBS' - Currently, a capital coverage of 60% applies to foreign participations
## Key facts - **What**: New rules on foreign participations of systemic banks - When: 31 August 2026 - Where: Economic Affairs and Taxation Committee of the Council of States (Bern) - Who: CET-S (chairman Erich Ettlin, Centre/OW) - Amount: 50% coverage in CET-1 + 50% in AT1 (vs. federal proposal of 100% CET-1) - Votes: 10 in favour, 2 against
### The Committee's decision
Bern, 31 August 2026. The Economic Affairs and Taxation Committee of the Council of States (CET-S) has approved a new regulation on foreign participations of large Swiss banks. According to the committee, systemic institutions — currently mainly UBS — must be subject to stricter rules on the coverage of these investments, but not at the level required by the Federal Council.
The Federal Council had proposed a coverage requirement of 100% through Common Equity Tier 1 (CET-1) own funds. The CET-S opted for a compromise: banks will cover half of their foreign participations with CET-1 own funds, and the other half through so-called AT1 bonds (Additional Tier 1). These are hybrid instruments that offer a high yield and can be converted into equity or declared worthless in the event of the company's distress — a scenario similar to what happened during the Credit Suisse crisis.
The committee vote recorded 10 votes in favour and 2 against. CET-S chairman Erich Ettlin (Centre/OW) stressed at a press conference that the decision represents 'a compromise' and not a gift to UBS. The purchase of AT1 entails costs for the bank, but Ettlin specified that the amount of such costs remains to be defined. The bank itself had strongly opposed the government proposal.
Today, banks must maintain capital coverage of 60% for foreign participations. The new rule would raise this level, although it does not reach the total requirement requested by the Federal Council. Ettlin also communicated that the Committee was unable to examine the Public Liquidity Backstop mechanism during its work.
### Balancing protection and competitiveness
According to Ettlin, the Committee's choice aims to 'strengthen the rules to better protect taxpayers, but also to ensure that the economy is not subject to excessive regulation'. This balance is central to the debate on Swiss banking supervision: on the one hand, the need to protect the financial system and savers from systemic risks; on the other, the concern that overly restrictive rules could compromise the international competitiveness of Swiss institutions. ### What AT1 Bonds Are and Why They Matter
To understand the CET-S compromise, one must first clarify the nature of AT1 bonds. Unlike Common Equity Tier-1 (CET-1) capital, which represents the most stable core capital of a bank, AT1 instruments are hybrid securities. They offer interest rates higher than conventional bonds, but they carry significant risks for those who hold them.
During the Credit Suisse crisis, AT1 bonds were declared worthless — a rare event that concretely demonstrated how these instruments do not guarantee capital safety. In the event of a bank's difficulties, the investor holding AT1s may lose it all, or see them converted into shares with drastically reduced value. This is why their use as a form of capital coverage is controversial: they do not offer the same level of protection as CET-1.
The Federal Council's proposal (100% CET-1) was more stringent and would have required UBS to accumulate significant amounts of capital as reserves. The Commission, on the other hand, considered that partial recourse to AT1s would allow a balance between two competing needs: maintaining prudential oversight over liquidity and capital stability, without forcing the bank to retain abnormally large volumes of CET-1 — resources it could otherwise deploy in profitable activities.
### Implications for the National Banking System
This decision primarily concerns UBS, but it signals a broader stance by the Swiss supervisory authorities. The Council of States (and by extension the Swiss Parliament) intends to tighten the discipline on systemically important banks without, however, strangling them with excessive constraints. The Commission chose to also involve market instruments (the AT1s) within the perimeter of protection, entrusting the market with the pricing of the associated risks.
For savers and investors, this choice carries a dual implication. On the one hand, more stringent rules on foreign participations reduce the likelihood that a large bank will accumulate massive losses on foreign investments without adequate coverage. On the other, the use of AT1s introduces an element of uncertainty: those who hold these securities know that, in a severe banking crisis scenario, their investment could be wiped out or converted into shares at nominal value.
The current coverage level (60%, which the Commission intended to raise) represented a previous compromise. With the new rules — still to be approved in plenary session — the parameter will rise, better protecting the system from uncovered exposures. However, the fact that UBS is not required to cover 100% with CET-1 means that the bank will retain a certain flexibility in managing its balance sheet and investment strategies.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### What savers and investors need to know
This decision by the CET-S will have a long-term effect, as it still needs to be approved by the full Council of States and may be subject to further modifications. However, anyone holding deposits at UBS or owning Swiss bank securities should keep a few elements in mind.
First: the new rule is aimed at better protecting depositors from risks related to uncovered foreign participations. If applied, the rules will reduce the bank's unsecured exposure, which theoretically increases the security of deposits within the Swiss system. Second: if you hold AT1 instruments issued by UBS or other systemically important banks, be aware that the value of these instruments depends on the solvency of the issuing bank. In a financial stress scenario, the value of AT1 instruments can collapse or be wiped out, as happened with Credit Suisse.
Third: CET-S decisions reflect a global trend towards greater rigour in banking supervision. This is not an isolated phenomenon in Switzerland, but part of an international orientation. If you work in the financial sector, the new rules will entail stricter compliance requirements and demand close attention to internal risk management processes.
### Next steps and what to monitor
The Commission's decision, although important, is not yet law. The text must be submitted to the full Council of States for final approval. After the Council of States, the procedure will follow the ordinary legislative paths, possibly including a meeting with the National Council (the lower house of the Swiss Parliament). Further modifications may emerge during this process.
Ettlin also pointed out that the Commission did not have time to examine the Public Liquidity Backstop mechanism, an issue closely related to the protection of banking stability. This topic could return to the agenda in the future.
If you are a saver or investor interested in the dynamics of the Swiss financial sector, it is worth monitoring parliamentary developments over the coming months. You can consult the Swiss Parliament website or the official Confederation portal to follow the legislative process. In the meantime, if you hold AT1 instruments or other hybrid securities, assess the risk profile together with a qualified financial advisor. For broader planning of your wealth and pension situation, [use our financial planning calculator](nav:calculator) to analyse how your investment choices align with your long-term goals.
Finally, remember that decisions on banking supervision also indirectly affect bank competitiveness and profits, which in turn impact dividends and returns for shareholders. If you hold UBS shares, stay informed on how the new capital constraints could redefine the bank's capital return strategy. [Explore your banking investment options in Switzerland](nav:banks) to better orient yourself in the market.

item.title: Record income and savings in Switzerland in 2025
item.description: In 2025, the disposable income per inhabitant exceeds CHF 65,000. Voluntary savings rate at 19.3%, all-time high. UST data reveals the highest economic well-being ever.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - In 2025, disposable income per inhabitant exceeds 65,000 CHF (all-time high) - Voluntary savings rate reaches 19.3% for the first time - Growth of +36% since 1995 at purchasing power parity - Source: Federal Statistical Office (FSO)
## Key facts - **What**: Disposable income and voluntary savings reach all-time highs - When: 2025 - Where: Switzerland (national average) - Who: Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Amount: 65,124 CHF per inhabitant (disposable income) - Savings rate: 19.3% voluntary, 27.4% overall - Growth 1995-2025: 36% net of inflation
For the first time, adjusted disposable income per inhabitant has exceeded 65,000 francs and the voluntary savings rate of households has reached 19.3%, an all-time high in the series. The Federal Statistical Office has published official data on the financial situation of Swiss households for 2025, and the figures are striking for their absolute records.
Adjusted disposable income per inhabitant reached exactly 65,124 CHF in 2025. In the same year, the voluntary savings rate hit 19.3%, a level never recorded before in the entire FSO historical series. These figures do not represent a one-off anomaly, but rather the confirmation of a multi-decade trend of steady growth.
Over the past thirty years, adjusted disposable income per inhabitant has grown uninterruptedly. Since 1995, when it stood at 40,083 francs, growth at purchasing power parity reaches almost 36%. The average purchasing power of the Swiss today is therefore well above that of a generation ago.
### How disposable income is measured
Adjusted disposable income of households per inhabitant is a fundamental economic indicator used to measure the material well-being and real purchasing power of citizens. It represents how much money remains with families after adding up all incomes and subtracting current taxes and social contributions, and adding the value of free or subsidised public services that citizens benefit from. This metric offers a much more accurate picture of the quality of life compared to the traditional gross disposable income.
The increase in housing costs, health insurance premiums and other mandatory expenses continues, however, to weigh on many Swiss households. Differences between regions, income brackets and types of households remain significant. Nevertheless, looking at the population as a whole, the long-term trend appears clear and unequivocal. ## The growth of savings: a singular phenomenon
Income growth is important, but the peculiarity that emerges when observing the behaviour of households is even more significant. While in many European countries the increase in income mainly translates into a growth in consumption, in Switzerland a growing share of resources is regularly set aside.
In 2025, the overall savings rate reached 27.4% of adjusted gross disposable income, compared with 19.6% in 1995. This means that more than a quarter of the resources available to households is allocated to the formation of savings. Every person living in Switzerland spent approximately 53,000 francs and set aside almost 18,000 francs, of which around 12,600 in the form of voluntary savings.
### The record of voluntary savings
For the first time in the history of data published by the FSO, the voluntary savings rate reached 19.3% in 2025, almost double the 9.7% recorded thirty years earlier. Voluntary savings represent the share that remains after considering not only consumption, but also the mandatory saving components linked to the pension system, such as contributions to the LPP occupational pension fund.
This figure shows a concrete and not merely theoretical financial capacity. Swiss households not only earn more, but also have ever greater margins to accumulate wealth, deal with unforeseen events and plan for the future with greater peace of mind.
### The effect of the pandemic and the persistence of the trend
The pandemic marked a turning point in the national propensity to save. After a phase of moderate growth between the end of the 1990s and the first decade of the 2000s, the propensity to save began to strengthen gradually starting from 2020. The limitations on consumption imposed by health measures led to an increase in household savings, a classic mechanism in periods of economic and social uncertainty.
However, once the health emergency came over, there was no return to previous levels. Savings continued to rise significantly, a sign of a financial capacity that has consolidated over the years. Financial crises, recessions, geopolitical tensions and a pandemic have not weakened the propensity to save, but have structurally strengthened it.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to leverage greater savings capacity
For Swiss families, access to an increasingly higher disposable income combined with a well-established propensity to save creates concrete opportunities for long-term financial planning. However, it is essential to act strategically: setting money aside without a clear direction is very different from building a structured savings plan based on specific goals.
The three priority areas are: pension planning through contributions to the LPP (pension fund), which remains the foundation of the Swiss pension system; optimisation of Pillar 3a, which offers significant tax benefits every year up to a defined maximum amount that can be deducted from the [tax return](nav:tax-return); and building a solid family budget to identify where to direct savings toward concrete goals such as retirement, emergencies, and purchasing a home.
### Key procedures and deadlines for savings
Each canton has slightly different rules regarding Pillar 3a, but at the federal level the deadlines remain uniform and well known. The annual tax return is the crucial moment to verify whether you are fully exploiting the deduction tools available for retirement savings. Many Swiss residents do not take full advantage of tax benefits at the cantonal and federal levels.
If you are an employee, the [family budget calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to simulate the impact of your pension contributions on gross disposable income and identify margins for optimisation. For self-employed individuals or those with diversified income, consulting a cantonal tax advisor remains useful to avoid missing structured savings and estate planning opportunities.
### Using data to plan the future
FSO data show that there is concrete room to save in Switzerland: the key now is to direct it toward specific goals rather than letting it be dispersed in everyday consumption. Use [our pension planning tools](nav:pension) and the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate your options and start planning your future financial well-being today.

item.title: Swiss banks, the CET-S restrains the Federal Council on equity capital
item.description: The Commission of the Council of States modifies the government's proposal: up to half of the coverage may come from AT1 bonds, not just from CET-1.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - CET-S slows down the 100% coverage in own funds for foreign subsidiaries - AT1 bonds could cover half of the required coverage - Currently the capital coverage for foreign participations is 60% - UBS is the only systemic bank today affected by the measure
## Key facts - **What**: The Commission for Economics and Taxes of the Council of States (CET-S) amends the Federal Council's proposal on the coverage of foreign participations of systemic banks - When: Debate and vote in Commission, announcement made in the evening via press conference - Where: Bern, Federal Palace - Who: CET-S, chaired by Erich Ettlin (Centre/OW); Federal Councillor Karin Keller-Sutter (Federal Department of Finance, FDF); Daniela Stoffel (State Secretariat for International Finance Matters, SIF) - How: Vote with 10 in favour, 2 against and 1 abstention - Original proposal: 100% coverage through Common Equity Tier 1 own funds (CET-1) - CET-S proposal: Partial coverage through AT1 bonds (Additional Tier 1), with a revision of their functioning - Current regime: Capital coverage of 60% for foreign participations
The Commission for Economics and Taxes of the Council of States (CET-S) has decided not to impose on the large Swiss banks a full 100% coverage in Common Equity Tier 1 own funds (CET-1) for their foreign subsidiaries, as proposed by the Federal Council within the framework of the revision of the banking law. The Commission prefers instead to allow about half of the coverage to be guaranteed through the so-called AT1 bonds (Additional Tier 1), hybrid instruments that offer a high yield but that can be converted into own capital or declared worthless in the event of difficulties of the issuing company — a mechanism that became known to the general public during the Credit Suisse affair.
The CET-S however requests a revision of the AT1 bonds, so that their loss-absorption effect is quicker. Measures are also envisaged aimed at preventing a bank from issuing these securities when it is already in a precarious financial situation, to avoid that the rescue instrument itself becomes a source of risk.
### Own capital and consequences in case of failure to meet the requirements
The CET-S has also defined what happens if a bank should no longer be able to meet the 'hard' own capital requirements. In these cases, the obligation to suspend the payment of dividends to shareholders and the repurchase of shares will kick in. The bonuses paid to executives will have to be reduced, or even suppressed, depending on the extent and duration of the failure to meet the capital requirements. The decision was taken at the end of a debate held in the presence of Federal Councillor Karin Keller-Sutter, head of the Federal Department of Finance (FDF), and of Daniela Stoffel, head of the State Secretariat for International Finance Matters (SIF). The final vote recorded 10 in favour, 2 against and 1 abstention. The Commission did not have time to examine the state Public Liquidity Backstop mechanism, a topic that remains open. ### The reasons for the compromise: why not 100% CET-1
CET-S President Erich Ettlin summarized the philosophy behind the decision with an explicit formula: 'We want to strengthen the rules to better protect taxpayers, but also to ensure that the economy is not subjected to excessive regulation.' It is a balance between two needs: on the one hand, the protection of financial stability and public funds; on the other, the preservation of the international competitiveness of the Swiss financial center. Ettlin then made clear that this is 'a compromise — and not a gift to UBS': the purchase of AT1 bonds nevertheless involves costs, even though, he admitted, it is not clear how much these bonds would cost the number one Swiss bank. The bank had strongly opposed the original government proposal.
In concrete terms, the difference between the Federal Council's April proposal and the CET-S variant is not marginal. The Federal Council was asking that systemically important banks — today, in fact, only UBS would be affected — fully finance their foreign subsidiaries with Common Equity Tier 1 capital (CET-1). CET-S instead proposes that half of the coverage be met through AT1 bonds, a capital instrument that nevertheless has varying degrees of subordination and conversion risk depending on the issuing terms.
### Comparison between the regimes: from 60% to the mixed scenario
To grasp the scope of the change, it may be useful to compare the regimes side by side.
| Regime | Required coverage for foreign participations | Main instrument | |---|---|---| | Current (in force) | 60% | Own capital (composition not detailed in the source) | | Federal Council proposal (April) | 100% | CET-1 only (Common Equity Tier 1 funds) | | CET-S proposal | To be defined in the texts | CET-1 + AT1 bonds (up to about 50%) |
The shift from a 60% regime to a scenario involving AT1 bonds directly affects the liability structure of Swiss systemically important banks, because AT1 bonds are subordinated securities that pay higher coupons than ordinary capital but offer, in return, the possibility of conversion into shares or write-down in the event of a crisis. For outside observers, this means that a larger share of the financing of foreign branches will be absorbed by bond investors rather than by shareholders.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What changes in practice: possible scenarios
The CET-S text is not yet law: it is a Commission decision that must now go through the parliamentary process. The Commission itself stated that it did not have time to examine the Public Liquidity Backstop mechanism, pointing out that the dossier is still open.
Based on the factual data contained in the source, a few explicit scenarios can be hypothesized, presented as such and not as certain predictions:
Scenario A — A fully compliant systemic bank. A bank that meets all capital requirements can continue to pay dividends, repurchase its own shares, and award bonuses to executives without restrictions. No automatic obligation to issue additional AT1.
Scenario B — A bank falling below requirements. The obligation to suspend dividends and share buybacks kicks in; executive bonuses are reduced or, in the most serious cases, eliminated. The duration and extent of the reduction depend on how long and to what extent the requirements are not met.
Scenario C — Issuing AT1 while in difficulty. The CET-S explicitly provides measures to prevent a bank from issuing AT1 bonds when it is already in a precarious financial situation: in other words, the instrument designed to strengthen capital cannot be used as a last resort.
### How to follow the evolution of the dossier
For those who live or work in Switzerland and want to follow the legislative process of the bank law revision, the operational steps are the following, based exclusively on the information contained in the source:
- Consult the CET-S Council of States press releases to know the text that the Commission will propose to the upper Chamber. - Check the subsequent developments of the dossier, in particular the examination of the Public Liquidity Backstop, which the Commission declared it has not yet had time to examine. - Follow the process in the Council of States and, subsequently, the procedure to eliminate divergences with the National Council, as well as the final stage at the Federal Council.
The concrete impact for Swiss taxpayers, as Ettlin stressed, is the stated objective of "strengthening the rules to better protect taxpayers": the CET-S decision moves in this direction, through a compromise that combines "hard" own funds (CET-1) and hybrid instruments (AT1) with automatic mechanisms suspending dividends and bonuses in case of breach of capital requirements. The final decision now lies with the Council of States.
To learn more about income and asset protection mechanisms in Switzerland, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator).

item.title: Droughts and purifiers: rivers in crisis
item.description: Swiss rivers drained by drought: wastewater remains constant. In Aargau up to 80% of the flow is contaminated purified water. Federal program 2024-2040 to upgrade 140 plants.

item.title: Zurich bans headscarves and cell phones in schools
item.description: The Zurich Grand Council approves the ban on headscarves and mobile phones by a narrow margin. Aargau had already decided on the veil. Times: two years for laws.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Zurich approves veil and mobile phone ban at school with narrow votes (87-82, 92-82) - Aargau had already approved veil ban a week earlier (78-54) - Zurich government has 2 years to develop laws compliant with Constitution
## Key facts - **What**: Ban on wearing veils in public schools/kindergartens for girls and women; ban on mobile phones in mandatory education - When: Approvals today by Zurich Grand Council; Aargau a week earlier - Where: Canton Zurich and Canton Aargau - Who: UDC (veil motion), UDC + UDF (mobile phone postulate), State Councils - Votes: 87 in favor-82 against-6 abstentions (veil); 92 in favor-82 against-2 abstentions (mobile phones)
The Zurich Grand Council approved today, with a narrow margin of 87 votes against 82 and six abstentions, a controversial motion by the Union of the Center that calls for a ban on wearing veils for girls and women in all public schools and kindergartens in the canton. Before the parliamentary debate, the Zurich State Council had already indicated its readiness to accept the motion and to draw up legislation compliant with the Constitution. The government now has two years to submit to Parliament a report and a legislative proposal.
The decision comes a week after the Aargau Grand Council had already accepted a similar motion, with 78 votes in favor and 54 against, tasking the cantonal government with drawing up a ban for female students of mandatory education up to the age of 16. In Aargau, however, the State Council had opposed it, arguing that legal obstacles exist, constitutional reservations and issues related to the jurisprudence of the Federal Court.
In the same session today, the Zurich Grand Council approved a second measure: with 92 votes in favor, 82 against and two abstentions, a postulate by the UDC and the Union of Democratic Forces passed, which calls for an absolute ban on mobile phones in mandatory education. The State Council will have to assess the adoption of binding guidelines at cantonal level, also with a two-year deadline to draw up a report.
### Current situation: variety among municipalities
So far, individual Zurich municipalities have addressed the issue of digital devices in [kindergartens](nav:nursery) and school institutions in very different ways, leaving room for fragmented local decisions. The mobile phone ban, as provided for in the approved postulate, would concern smartphones, tablets and notebooks at all levels, from kindergarten to the end of ninth grade. Crucial: the ban would not only apply during lessons, but also during breaks and in all day care facilities and support structures of schools and municipalities.
However, the postulate provides for some specific exceptions: the ban does not apply for documented health reasons. Also excluded are devices managed directly by the school and necessary for carrying out the lessons themselves. This means that if a female teacher uses a didactic tablet, or if a teacher uses devices for integrated learning, these remain permitted. ### Cantonal uniformity against local fragmentation
The approval of the two Zurich measures represents a significant change compared to the current fragmented situation. Today each municipality decides independently: some allow phones in breaks, others ban them completely, others still establish limitations for certain age groups. Cantonal legislation will create a uniform standard, eliminating municipal disparities and ensuring consistency throughout Zurich.
As for the veil, the Zurich decision represents a further strengthening compared to the Argovian motion: it is not limited to compulsory schooling until the age of 16, but extends the ban to all girls and women in schools and public kindergartens without specific age restrictions. This means that even high school students would be subject to the ban, a wider scope than in Aargau.
For families and students, this uniformity has advantages and disadvantages that affect the [qualità della vita e del vivere in Svizzera](nav:cost-of-living). Regulatory certainty avoids confusion between municipalities, but at the same time reduces local flexibility and could clash with the specific needs of certain school contexts or individual situations.
### The Remaining Constitutional Issues
The opposition of the Argovian State Council highlighted legal obstacles and constitutional reservations, with explicit references to the jurisprudence of the Federal Court. Although the Board of
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### How Zurich Schools Will Change
If the cell phone ban were implemented, each Zurich school would need to comply with binding cantonal guidelines. School administrations would have to develop clear procedures for collecting and storing devices during school hours, communicate the new rules to parents and students, and define consequences for non-compliance. Health-related exceptions would require advance medical documentation from parents or guardians.
For the veil ban, if approved after the legislative process, school administrations would need to review internal regulations and communicate the change to affected families and students. Although the Zurich government has stated it will draft a constitutionally compliant law, the process remains complex and subject to possible legal challenges that could delay practical implementation.
Teachers and school principals will need specific training on how to implement the bans consistently, fairly, and respectfully. Schools will also need to address concrete situations: how to communicate the ban to students, how to manage initial resistance, how to handle potential conflicts with families.
### What to Do Now: Parents, Students, and Teachers
For Zurich parents and students, the practical advice is straightforward: at least until the State Council presents its report (not before two years), current rules remain in effect. Each school will continue to apply its own local policies on cell phones and head coverings. The approved motions are not yet law; they represent only a mandate to the government to develop proposals.
Those living in other cantons should monitor their respective Grand Council decisions: Switzerland remains fragmented on these issues. If the Zurich-Argovia model were to spread, other cantons could follow in the coming years, but currently each canton maintains its own autonomy in school matters.
### Next Steps: The Role of the Zurich State Council
The Zurich State Council must now begin work on drafting two separate reports: one on the veil ban in public schools and kindergartens, one on the cell phone ban in compulsory education. These reports will need to address questions of administrative feasibility, constitutional compliance, implementation costs, and likely consultations with concerned municipalities and school stakeholders.
Once presented to Parliament (within two years), genuine public and parliamentary debates will begin, where amendments could modify the terms of the bans. It is essential to follow official updates to understand how today's approved motions will translate into actual legislation.

item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - LPP Commission recommends 1.75% minimum rate for 2027 - 0.50 percentage point increase from current 1.25% - Final mark: 10 votes to 4 - Final decision rests with the Federal Council
## Key facts - **What**: Recommendation to increase the minimum interest rate LPP - When: 31 August 2026 (recommendation for 2027) - Where: Bern - Who: Federal Commission on Occupational Welfare (LPP Commission) - From: 1.25% (current rate) - A: 1.75% (proposed rate) - Change: +0.50 percentage points - Vote: 10 in favour, 4 against
The Federal Commission on Occupational Pensions (LPP Commission) recommends to the Federal Council to raise the minimum occupational pension interest rate to 1.75 percent by 2027. The projected increase is 0.50 percentage points compared to the current rate of 1.25 percent. The recommendation was formalized on August 31, 2026 in Bern, at the end of the final vote that recorded 10 votes in favor and 4 against.
### The criteria behind the decision
The Commission examined three options: increase, maintain or reduce the rate. The law indicates as fundamental parameters the performance of the Confederation's bonds and the performance of shares, bonds and real estate. Financial markets showed a positive trend in 2025 and, so far, also in 2026.
In addition to market returns, the Commission assessed The change from 1.25% to 1.75% marks a substantial increase in the minimum return that pension institutions must pay on old age in the compulsory occupational pension scheme (LPP/BVG). The Commission itself defines the increase as "considerable", indicating a willingness to reflect the good financial situation of the sector, while maintaining a margin of caution in the face of geopolitical uncertainties.
### What the minimum rate actually means
The minimum interest rate LPP is the minimum guaranteed return that each pension institution must credit on the old age of policyholders in the mandatory scheme. An increase of 0.50 percentage points affects the annual revaluation of pension accounts: all other things being equal, a higher credit score generates, year after year, a faster growth in the capital allocated to income.
The proposed rate is a minimum. The joint supreme body of each pension fund — composed equally of representatives of employers and workers — may decide on a higher rate, provided that the financial sustainability of the institution allows it. This means that individual funds with solid capital returns could offer more favorable conditions to their policyholders than the federal benchmark.
### The market context
The recommendation is part of a scenario characterized by financial markets in positive territory

1. The LPP Commission formulates the recommendation (which took place on 31 August 2026). 2. The file is examined by the UFAS/BSV, which operates under the supervision of the DFI. 3. The Federal Council evaluates the proposal and decides on a possible change to the minimum interest rate. 4. The decision is published and enters into force with the planned effective date (for 2027, according to the recommendation).
### What to do as an LPP-insured worker
- Check with your employer or pension fund the interest rate currently applied to your retirement savings in the mandatory scheme. - Consult your personal pension certificate, which indicates the interest rate and the year-by-year evolution of your retirement savings. - Follow the official communications from your institution, which will have to adapt to any new rate set by the Federal Council. - If in doubt, contact your trade union or the joint body of the pension fund for clarifications on the application of the rate.
### Difference between the minimum rate and the effective rate
The recommended rate of 1.75% is a legal minimum. The supreme joint body of your pension fund can decide on a higher rate if the financial situation of the institution allows it. It is therefore possible that the rate actually credited to your retirement savings is higher than the federal parameter.
### When to expect the final decision
The Federal Council is not bound by either the timing or the content of the recommendation. The reduction cuts across both major sectors: in the private sector the unexplained part was 6.7%, i.e. 644 francs per month, compared with 7.2% and 653 francs in 2022; in the public sector it was 5.9%, or 574 francs per month on average, versus 6.7% and 623 francs in 2022. This is the share that, according to the FSO definition, cannot be statistically attributed to differences in education, seniority, or hierarchical position.
### Where the Gap Is Widest
The differences are particularly evident in specific sectors. The unexplained component amounted to 191 francs in accommodation and food services, 606 francs in retail, 829 francs in the manufacture of machinery and equipment, and 1,506 francs in financial and insurance activities. The latter figure is roughly 2.4 times higher than that of the manufacturing sector and almost eight times higher than that of accommodation and food services. For workers in the financial and insurance sector, the residual gap is therefore the largest in absolute value.
### Company Size, Hierarchy, Age
More generally, the unexplained component of the pay gap is more pronounced in small businesses. It also tends to increase with hierarchical level: the higher you climb within a company, the larger the gap. The difference also widens as the age of employees increases. Finally, the FSO found differences based on marital status. Among unmarried employees, the unexplained component of the pay gap was 2.7% in 2024, compared with 2.8% in 2022. Among married individuals it reached 8.1%, versus 8.8% in 2022.
### Implications for Those Working in Switzerland
For those employed in Switzerland, this figure fits into a labour market context in which pay differences are also measured against the cost of living and pension contributions. An unexplained component of 640 gross francs per month has a direct impact on AVS/LPP contributions paid, on the calculation of future pensions, and on the capacity to save. Those earning higher salaries — for example in the financial and insurance sector, where the unexplained component exceeds 1,500 francs — suffer the most significant absolute loss, even if in percentage terms the public sector remains the one with the historically highest structural share.
### 'Before and After' Scenario
Between 2022 and 2024 the reduction was 0.5 percentage points in the overall figure (from 16.2% to 15.7%), 0.3 points in the private sector (from 17.5% to 17.2%), and 1.0 point in the public sector (from 13.8% to 12.8%). The overall gap between the private and public sectors remains wide (4.4 percentage points in 2024), but the public sector has reduced the gap more markedly than the private sector. ## Key facts - **What**: SES electricity tariff reduction for the third consecutive year - When: Year 2027 - Where: Ticino, Mesolcina and Calanca (SES area) - Who: Società Elettrica Sopracenerina SA (Locarno office) - Ticino savings: 53 CHF equivalent to about 4% - Mesolcin/Calanca savings: 73 CHF equivalent to 5.5% - Average consumption: 4,500 kilowatt hours per year
The downward trend in tariffs for customers of Società Elettrica Sopracenerina SA continues. In 2027, for the third consecutive year, SES reports a decline in energy bills thanks to a reduction in supply costs and efficient portfolio management.
In the Ticino area of SES, an average domestic economy with an annual consumption of 4,500 kilowatt hours will save 53 francs, equivalent to about 4%. An even more significant reduction concerns the four municipalities of lower Mesolcina and Calanca served by Sopracenerina: here the drop reaches 73 francs, or 5.5%.
### Tariff structure unchanged, but with specific variations
The tariff structure remains stable compared to 2026. The bill continues to be composed of five elements: network use, metering rate, supply of ### Smart meter: adjustment of the metering tariff
The metering tariff, introduced for the first time in 2026, will be adjusted from CHF 6.10 to CHF 6.30 per month — an increase of CHF 0.20 monthly, equivalent to CHF 2.40 annually. This adjustment is linked to the expected costs of accelerating the replacement of traditional meters with intelligent models (smart meters), in compliance with the current federal regulatory framework.
The smart meter represents an investment in transparency and energy efficiency: it allows customers to monitor consumption in real time, promoting conscious energy use and facilitating the integration of local renewable sources. The installation and management of these devices involve costs that SES gradually transfers to the bill.
For most customers, the CHF 2.40 annual increase is fully offset by the reduction on the energy supply. In fact, the balance is largely positive: the net savings remain at CHF 53 in Ticino or CHF 73 in Mesolcina and Calanca.
### The decisive drop: energy supply
The component that really makes the difference is the energy supply. Compared to 2026, the cost of this item will decrease by approximately 13% for SES customers in Ticino and by about 16% for customers in Graubünden. This drop is significant: while 3% increases on the grid and the smart meter adjustment absorb part of the savings, the energy reduction represents the largest net gain.
SES attributes this result to two strategic factors: the procurement strategy made it possible to minimize the volatility of energy prices over recent months; the well-balanced portfolio of Sopracenerina, characterized by a mix of locally produced renewable energy and energy purchased on the wholesale market.
In practice, thanks to careful management and diversification between local sources and the market, SES has transferred to customers the advantage of lower energy prices in 2027. This approach protected customers from global energy volatility, avoiding steeper increases.

In the context of the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), energy represents a significant item in the family budget. A reduction of CHF 53-73 per year is not marginal: for an average family with standard consumption, it equates to a discount of about 4-5.5% on overall energy spending. ## In a nutshell - In 2025 the PS raised 7.9 million francs, the highest among federal parties - Nine parties declare a total of 24.6 million, down by 1 million compared to 2024 - Mandatory transparency for parties represented in the Federal Assembly
## Key facts - **What**: Revenue declared by Swiss federal parties in 2025 - When: Data published by the Federal Financial Control in 2025 - Where: Swiss Federal Assembly - Who: Federal Financial Control (FFC) - Most Revenue Party: PS with CHF 7.9 million - Total declared: 24.6 million francs (9 parties) - Change: -1 million compared to 2024
## # Political Funding Numbers
The Federal Financial Controller has made public the data on the revenue declared by nine of the ten parties represented in the Federal Assembly for the year 2025. Altogether, the amounts amount to 24.6 million francs, a figure that marks a contraction of about one million compared to the 25.6 million declared in 2024. Leading the national ranking is the Socialist Party (PS) with 7.9 million francs, confirming the party with the highest income ever.
Behind the PS are the Radical Liberal Party (PLR) with 4.8 million, the Centre Democratic Union (UDC) with 3.8 million and the Centre with 2.7 million. The Greens declared 1.8 million francs, while the Liberal Greens stand at 1.2 million. The Remaining Parties — Democratic Union ### What emerges from the data
The overall contraction of one million francs between 2024 and 2025 deserves attention. If the SP maintained absolute leadership, its loss of 0.3 million suggests a slight erosion in fundraising capacity. More relevant is the decline in the PLR, which lost as much as 1.8 million: the figure represents almost 27 percent of the radical party's overall revenue, signaling a significant reduction in its funding base.
Otherwise, the UDC has been able to increase its revenues by 1.0 million francs, a result that positions it as one of the few winners of this round. The Centre, despite having earned only 0.1 million, has at least confirmed a stability in its cash flows. Among the smaller parties, the situation remains more contained. The Greens, with 1.8 million, remain the third pole after PS and PLR for declared revenue volumes, while the liberal Greens are significantly different with 1.2 million.
The lack of data related to the Ticinese League complicates the national picture: not knowing how much this formation has collected prevents having a complete picture of federal political funding in 2025.
### What counts as "revenue"
Importantly, the figures released by the Federal Financial Control do not include all cash flows to parties. Mandatory declarations relate to income from donations, events, sales

In Switzerland, the obligation to be transparent about party funding is one of the pillars of federal democracy. Parties that have representation in the Federal Assembly must submit their entry data to public scrutiny every year, according to the rules on the transparency of policy funding. This mechanism allows citizens and researchers to verify the economic sources of the main national political actors.
The Federal Financial Control acts as the body responsible for the collection, verification and publication of this data. The annual reports make the totality of declared revenues public, allowing a cross-cutting view of how parties finance themselves. Access to this information is guaranteed: anyone wishing to consult the data can do so through the official channels of the federal administration.
However, as the current data has shown, transparency has structural limitations. Not all political formations with federal representation declare promptly (the case of the Ticinese League demonstrates this), and the possibility for parties to pay funds through their cantonal structures creates grey areas in the overall framework.

item.title: Apprenticeship in Graubünden: dual path, AFC and CFC
item.description: Apprenticeship in Graubünden: dual school-company system regulated by the LFPr, AFC and CFC qualifications, salary and professional maturity to access the SUPPL.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - Apprenticeship in Switzerland: dual pathway (school + company) regulated at the federal level - Vocational education and training in Graubünden: coordinated offer by the Canton and the Confederation - Vocational baccalaureate: pathway following the apprenticeship for access to universities of applied sciences (FACH) - Apprentice remuneration: set by the Canton/Vocational Education Office, differs by year and sector
## Key facts - **What**: Apprenticeship and vocational education in the Canton of Graubünden - When: current training year (exact dates not specified in the source) - Where: Canton of Graubünden, with reference to the Swiss national framework - Who: Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training of Graubünden (name not specified in the source) - How: dual school-company pathway under the VPETA (Federal Act on Vocational Education and Training) - Final qualification: AFC (Federal Certificate of Competence) or CFC (Federal Diploma of VET), depending on duration - Vocational baccalaureate: accessible after the apprenticeship to continue at a university of applied sciences (FACH)
Vocational education and training is the most common post-compulsory pathway in Switzerland, and in the Canton of Graubünden it operates under the same federal legal bases that govern the rest of the country. The VPETA and its related ordinance set the qualifications that can be awarded, the standard durations, and the relationship between vocational school and host company. In the Canton of Graubünden, implementation is the responsibility of the Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training, which coordinates the supply of apprenticeship places, vocational schools and federal examinations.
An apprenticeship is run in dual form: three or four days a week in the company and one or two days at vocational school, plus inter-company courses. The source indicates as final qualifications the AFC (attestato federale di capacità) issued after a two-year pathway (abbreviated training, more practice-oriented), and the CFC (certificato federale di capacità) issued after three or four years (more in-depth training with a solid theoretical foundation). Those who obtain an AFC can progress towards an abbreviated CFC, in accordance with cantonal equivalence rules.
### Where to find an apprenticeship in Graubünden The search for an apprenticeship goes through the usual channels of the Swiss system: the national professions portal (orientamento.ch), the regional placement offices (URC) active in Graubünden, the cantonal platforms managed by the Office for Vocational Education and Training, and the direct channels of host companies. Applications are generally submitted with standard dossiers (CV, cover letter, latest school report and summer work certificates). For available positions in Graubünden, [consult the active job listings](nav:jobs). The Swiss dual system offers concrete advantages for both young people and training companies. From the trainee's perspective, the apprenticeship allows earning an income during training, gaining real work experience, and obtaining a federally recognised qualification valued in the labour market. From the companies' perspective, it represents a structured recruitment channel, with contribution relief and the ability to train personnel according to their own needs. In Graubünden, where the economic fabric is characterised by small and medium-sized enterprises in the tourism, construction, crafts, and public services sectors, the apprenticeship remains one of the main gateways into the working world.
On the economic side, the apprentice's salary is set according to cantonal recommendations, which in Graubünden are published by the Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training and vary by apprenticeship year and sector. The remuneration takes into account the fact that the trainee already produces part of the added value within the company while continuing their school education in parallel. The salary deductions applied follow federal rules: OASI/DI/IC 5.3% borne by the employee (10.6% total with employer), unemployment insurance 1.1% up to the annual ceiling, and LAA/UVLA between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector of activity. These contributions are not optional and also apply to apprentices hired under an apprenticeship contract.
### Federal vocational maturity and subsequent pathways After obtaining the CFC (Federal Certificate of Competence), it is possible to access the federal vocational maturity, a qualification that opens the doors to the Universities of Applied Sciences (UAS/UAS). In Graubünden, preparation for the federal vocational maturity is offered by the cantonal vocational schools, often in the form of a course parallel to the third or fourth year of apprenticeship (integrated model) or as an additional year after the diploma (post-CFC model). This option is particularly relevant for those who intend to continue their studies without going through a liceo/gymnasium.
An often overlooked aspect concerns the trainee's insurance cover during the apprenticeship: as an employee, they are insured against occupational and non-occupational accidents through the employer (UVL/LAA) and, as a resident, are required to take out health insurance under the LAMal within three months of arrival in Switzerland (or of starting work) — an aspect that may concern cross-border apprentices or those coming from other cantons.
In terms of contractual rights, the apprentice benefits from the federal labour legislation applicable in all cantons: a maximum weekly working time of 45 hours in industry/office/sales sectors and 50 hours in other sectors, minimum holiday of four weeks (five for those under 20), and protection against abusive dismissal under the Code of Obligations. There is no federal minimum wage, and in Graubünden no cantonal minimum wage is currently in force.
From a tax perspective, apprentices with their own income are subject to federal direct tax (IFD), cantonal tax, and municipal tax, according to the three-level system in force throughout Switzerland. To fill in the tax return, [use the tax return guide](nav:tax-return). To simulate the impact of gross/net salary, [open the salary calculator](nav:calculator).
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). Obtaining an apprenticeship position in Graubünden requires a structured process. Here are the concrete steps to follow, based on the standard procedures of the Swiss vocational training system.
### Step-by-step application procedure 1. Identify the desired profession by consulting the national professions catalogue at orientamento.ch. 2. Prepare an updated CV, a personalised cover letter, and gather your last two school reports. 3. Check the listings published on the Graubünden cantonal portal and contact companies in the field directly. 4. Attend selection interviews bringing, if possible, certificates of internships or summer work experience. 5. Once you have secured a position, sign the apprenticeship contract: the document involves three parties (apprentice, company, and Canton) and specifies the profession, duration, schedule, remuneration, and the rights and duties of the parties. 6. Enrol at the relevant vocational school through the Graubünden Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training.
### Deadlines and useful documents Applications for the following training year are typically concentrated between September and February of the preceding year. The Canton publishes annual salary recommendations for apprentices, broken down by apprenticeship year and sector. For updated figures, it is necessary to consult directly the website of the Graubünden Cantonal Office for Vocational Education and Training, as the precise amounts vary from year to year.
For those coming from abroad, it is advisable to also check the permit regime: a non-EU/EFTA foreign apprentice requires a B residence permit issued by the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration), tied to the signing of the apprenticeship contract.

To assess your future salary or the tax impact of apprentice income, [use the salary calculator](nav:calculator). ## In a nutshell - Real estate purchase in Switzerland: 6-12 months from research to transcription - Minimum own funds: usually 20% of the purchase price - Acquisition tax and notary fees vary by canton and municipality - Mortgage mortgage sustainability assessed on income capacity
## Key facts - **What**: Residential purchase in Switzerland - When: Process 6-12 months - Where: Canton of Graubünden - Who: Buyer, bank, notary, cantonal land registers - Regulations: Federal Bond Code - Cost base: Mortgage + acquisition taxes + notary fees + transcription
### The real estate buying process in Switzerland
The purchase of a house in Switzerland follows a process governed by the Federal Bond Code, with cantonal variations on taxation and procedures. The Canton of Graubünden, like all cantons, applies its own rates on acquisition taxes and regulates notarial expenses according to cantonal tariffs.
The main phases are: property search, price negotiation, bank pre-qualification to verify the sustainability of the loan, stipulation of the notarial contract (mandatory), and transcription in the cantonal land registers. Each stage involves specific legal costs and responsibilities.
### Who leads the process: bank, notary and registers
The Swiss bank evaluates the sustainability of the mortgage loan on the basis of the buyer's income capacity, applying a stress-test that simulates scenarios of rising ### Mortgage financing: own funds and sustainability
Access to the mortgage loan in Switzerland requires own funds (usually 20% of the purchase price) and borrowing capacity (sufficient income for mortgage installments and other charges). A lower own fund percentage is possible at some banks, but it comes with a premium mortgage and significant additional costs.
Swiss banks assess the borrowing capacity on the buyer's gross income, deducting [assicurazione malattia obbligatoria (LAMal/KVG)](nav:health), [contributi previdenziali AVS/LPP](nav:pension), federal/cantonal/municipal taxes and other charges. They also apply a stress-test, simulating a high interest rate (usually +1-2%) to verify the sustainability of the mortgage in the scenario of rising rates decided by the Swiss National Bank (SNB). This conservative approach aims to avoid over-indebtedness of buyers.
### Fixed and variable rates
The loan can be variable rate (linked to market rates and the SNB's monetary policy) or fixed (contracted for 3, 5, 10+ years). Floating rates are more flexible but expose you to upside risk; fixed rates offer certainty but usually at higher initial premiums. The choice depends on the personal risk profile and the business cycle.
### LAMal's weight on borrowing capacity
Compulsory health insurance (LAMal) varies by canton and risk profile. Monthly premiums (from about CHF 300 for high deductibles to CHF 400+ for
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### The step-by-step purchase procedure
1. **Search and negotiation** (1-6 months): Identify the property, verify its legal situation, and negotiate the price.
2. Bank pre-qualification (1-3 weeks): Contact the bank with income documentation to obtain a pre-qualification letter, which confirms the maximum mortgage accessible.
3. Notarial contract (1-3 weeks): The notary drafts the sale contract, verifies the property's legal situation (absence of liens, encumbrances, easements), and obtains the parties' signatures.
4. Mortgage disbursement and payment (1-2 weeks): The bank disburses the financing. The buyer transfers their own funds. The notary transfers the funds to the seller and initiates the registration.
5. Registration in the land registry (1-4 weeks): The cantonal registry office records the change of ownership. Only once registration is completed, the buyer becomes the legal owner of the property.
### Acquisition taxes and expenses: cantonal variability

### Parmelin's response to criticism from the agricultural world The President of the Confederation Guy Parmelin spoke on Sunday on the RTS news 19h30 to respond to the ### Fodder: the most immediate challenge for the agricultural sector In addition to financial aid, the main concern now concerns the supply of fodder for the coming winter. In the future, the emergency will concern the supply of fodder for the winter and the end of winter, "said the president of the Confederation.
The situation is made more complex by the fact that drought affects a large part of Europe. item.title: Apprenticeship and vocational training in Graubünden: a complete guide
item.description: Dual school-company model in the Graubünden: internship contract, salary per year, professional maturity and living costs for the apprentice.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Vocational training in Graubünden: dual path school + company - Internship contract governing duration, hours and remuneration - Professional maturity obtainable in parallel with the internship - Apprentice salary varies by training year and sector
## Key facts - **What**: Apprenticeship and vocational training in the Canton of Graubünden - Where: Canton of Graubünden (Switzerland), under the supervision of the Cantonal Office for Vocational Training - Who: Canton of Graubünden, Swiss Confederation, training companies, vocational schools - How: dual system (company + vocational school) regulated by the Federal Law on Vocational Training (LFPr) - Final title: federal certificate of ability (AFC) or federal certificate of practical training (CFP)
Vocational training in Switzerland is regulated at the federal level by the Law on Vocational Training (LFPr), which defines its principles, and finds concrete application in each Canton, including Graubünden. The Swiss system is based on the so-called "dual model": the apprentice carries out practical training in a company and theoretical training in a vocational school at the same time, with intercompany courses that complete the path.
### The internship contract
The internship contract is the document that governs the relationship between the apprentice (or his/her representative, if a minor) and the training company. Before the entry into force of the ### Professional maturity: an additional opportunity
Professional maturity (MP) is a secondary qualification II that is obtained in parallel with the internship. It is divided into seven areas (health, social, visual and applied arts, economics, technique, architecture and natural sciences) and is open to holders of a federal certificate of ability or, in some cases, during the last year of the internship for candidates who meet the school requirements.
Obtaining the MP allows access, without further examination, to professional university schools (SUPs) in the respective subject area. To enroll in a university (ETH or cantonal university), on the other hand, gymnasial maturity or the passing of a complementary exam is required.
### Apprentice living costs and conditions
The cost of living in Switzerland is high and has a real impact on an apprentice's monthly budget. Accommodation is one of the main items, regulated by federal law (art. 253 et seq. CO) the same in each canton. The security deposit can be a maximum of three months' rent, it must be paid into a restricted account in the tenant's name. The cancellation of the landlord requires the official cantonal form, and the tenant can dispute it within thirty days to the conciliation authority.
Health insurance (LAMal) is mandatory for anyone residing in Switzerland. People moving for internship must take out coverage within three months
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Concrete procedure: how to proceed step by step
Finding an apprenticeship position in the Canton of Graubünden requires following a reasoned sequence of steps, which should ideally be started well in advance of the beginning of the apprenticeship.
The first step is to identify the desired sector and profession, by consulting the professional profiles published by the Federal Office for Professional Education and Technology (UFFT/BFTB). For each profession, the description of the skills, the duration of the training, and the list of schools involved are available.
The second step consists of preparing a complete application, made up of a cover letter, an updated CV, copies of school certificates and, where available, internship certificates or references. The cover letter should be tailored to the company and the chosen profession. In the most sought-after sectors, it is useful to apply to several companies, both directly and through job placement portals.
The third step is attending an exploratory interview, during which the company assesses the candidate's aptitudes and the candidate evaluates the work environment. Once the interview is passed, the parties sign an apprenticeship contract drawn up in writing and compliant with cantonal law.
The fourth step is the registration of the contract with the cantonal office for professional education in Graubünden, which verifies its compliance and enrolls the apprentice in the school pathway. The office also provides information on the planned inter-company courses.
### Deadlines and key moments
Applications for apprenticeship positions are concentrated in the autumn of the year preceding the start of the training. Companies publish vacancies starting from late summer and conduct interviews during the autumn months. Enrolments for the school subjects at the vocational school generally take place by the end of the year.
For holders of a B or C permit, the right of access to an apprenticeship is equal to that of Swiss citizens, subject to sectoral exceptions. For holders of a G permit, employment in Switzerland is linked to the cross-border employment relationship, and an apprenticeship is only possible if the job is carried out mainly in the canton's area of work.
### Useful tools and practical information
For those approaching vocational education and training in Switzerland, it is useful to consult the Confederation's berufsberatung.ch portal, which offers career guidance tests and detailed descriptions of the professions. In parallel, the orientamento.ch portal allows you to compare the access requirements for the different professions.
To estimate an apprentice's monthly budget (net salary, social contributions, accommodation, health insurance premiums) it is useful to use a dedicated calculator that takes into account the 5.3% AVS/AI/IPG deduction borne by the employee and the 1.1% for unemployment insurance, within the annual cap set by law. For LAMal premiums, the cantons publish each year the average premiums by region, useful as a starting reference.
Calculate your net salary in Switzerland with our [salary calculator](nav:calculator) and check in advance how much the apprentice will take home, taking into account taxes, contributions and health insurance premiums. For those who want to compare the job offers available in the canton, the site's [job listings](nav:jobs) section is also available.

item.title: Permit L in Graubünden: duration, extension and change of employer
item.description: In the Canton of Graubünden, the L permit lasts up to 12 months, extensions only in exceptional cases and change of employer subject to new cantonal application.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - L Permit: maximum duration of 12 months, not renewable as a rule - Issued by the Grison cantonal authorities for specific sectors - Change of employer subject to new cantonal application - Passage to permit B subject to regular stay and framework conditions
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term permit (L) issued by the Canton of Graubünden - When: duration up to 12 months, extensions only in exceptional cases - Where: Canton of Graubünden (competent cantonal authority) - Who: workers from third States or, under certain conditions, from EU/EFTA States - Amount: variable cantonal release fee (to be verified on the Canton's website) - Regulatory reference: Federal Law on Foreigners and related ordinance (LEI/OASA), cantonal application - Constraint: the L permit is closely linked to the employer and the reason for the release
In Switzerland, the short-term L permit is the legal instrument designed to cover temporary work needs, with a maximum duration of twelve months. In the Canton of Graubünden, the issuance is the responsibility of the cantonal migration office, which acts on the basis of the relevant federal legislation (Law on Foreigners and their Integration, LEI, and related OASA order) taking into account the cantonal particularities, in particular in terms of the labour market and quota.
The Swiss procedure distinguishes two main strands depending on the nationality of the The L permit in Graubünden is distinguished from other residence permits by two structural characteristics: the limited duration and the constraint on the employer. The combination of these two elements defines the area of use of the title and clearly differentiates it from the residence permit B, which is renewable and not linked to a single use, and from the residence permit C, which presupposes a long-term stay (normally ten years of residence, reduced to five for EU/EFTA citizens).
From an operational point of view, the L permit is closely connected to the reason for the issue and the employer indicated in the application. Any substantial change in the conditions — change of company, change of duties, extension beyond twelve months — requires in principle a new cantonal application, with reassessment of the case. The extension beyond the end of the twelve months is only provided for in exceptional situations provided for by federal legislation, for example in the event of a documented illness or accident that prevents the conclusion of the activity on time.
### Differences from permit B and concrete scenarios
The distinction between L and B has direct repercussions also in tax and social security matters. The holder of permit L, even if tax resident in the Canton of Graubünden, is subject to the ordinary Swiss structure, with direct federal tax (IFD), cantonal tax and municipal tax. The basis is income

Obtaining an L permit in the Canton of Graubünden requires following a precise procedural sequence, managed by the cantonal migration office. The application is not submitted by the individual worker, but by the future employer, who files the request by completing the required cantonal and federal forms and attaching the necessary documentation.
### Step-by-step procedure for the employer
The first step is gathering the worker's documents (valid passport, CV, training certificates, signed employment contract) and providing a detailed description of the intended position. The employer must demonstrate the temporary nature of the employment and its financial coverage. This is followed by a check with the competent cantonal labor market offices, aimed at ascertaining the priority of workers already registered as unemployed or residing in Switzerland. If the employment ends before the permit expires, the holder is required to report it to the cantonal office; a change of employer, even within the same canton, requires a new application, with a reassessment of the case. Extension beyond twelve months is allowed only in exceptional circumstances provided for by federal law, such as the continuation of an assignment for documented reasons not attributable to the will of the worker or the employer.
