item.title: Residence permit C Graubünden: requirements and application
item.description: The C permit is the permanent residence permit in Switzerland. Find out how to apply in the canton of Graubünden, the years of residence required, the tax implications, AVS/LPP and the path to ordinary naturalisation.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Permit C: permanent residence in Switzerland after 10 years (5 for EU/EFTA) - Managed by cantonal office Graubünden + Federal Secretariat of State for Migration (SEM) - It does not expire, unlike the B permit renewable every 5 years - Paves the way for ordinary naturalization after 10 years of full residency
## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit C — Swiss permanent residence license - Who: Issued by Canton Grisons + Federal Secretariat of State for Migration (SEM) - Requirements: 10 years ordinary residence in Switzerland; 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens - Naturalization: Permit C + 10 years total residence + cantonal/municipal requirements - Implications: Federal-cantonal-communal taxation; AVS/AI/LPP contributions; mandatory LAMal coverage
Residence permit C is the permanent residence permit in Switzerland, issued by the canton with validation by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) at the federal level. It represents the third level in permits for resident foreigners: after the L permit (short duration, up to 1 year) and the B permit (residence, renewable on a periodic basis).
Anyone who ordinarily resides in Switzerland for a minimum of 10 consecutive years can apply for the C permit. For citizens of the European Union and the European Free Trade Association (EU/EFTA), the term is reduced to 5 years. In the canton of Graubünden, as in every canton, the request is submitted to the competent cantonal office, the The C permit transforms the tax and social security position of the resident foreigner. First of all, with the C permit you become ** ordinary resident ** in Switzerland for federal, cantonal and municipal tax purposes. The Swiss tax calculator estimates the federal-cantonal taxation accurately based on the declared income.
### Federal, cantonal and municipal taxation
Direct Federal Tax (DFI) applies to the resident's worldwide income. The cantonal and municipal taxes of the canton of Graubünden follow the rates and multipliers of each municipality (the municipal multiplier applies to the cantonal tax base). Deductions may relate to AVS/AI/LPP contributions and payments to the third pillar 3a, subject to indexed annual ceilings. Each canton and municipality disseminates public tax tables: the canton of Graubünden publishes rates and multipliers for each municipality on the official website.
### Mandatory social security contributions
With the C permit, the resident is required to pay contributions towards the three pillars of social security. AVS/AI/IPG requires 5.3% to be paid by the employee (10.6% total with employer). The LPP (compulsory occupational pension from first employment) applies rates by age group: 7% for 25–34 years, 10% for 35–44, 15% for 45–54, 18% for 55+ up to the reference age. The [comparatore pensioni](nav:pension) helps to estimate future rent.
### Mandatory sickness coverage
Sickness coverage (LAMal/KVG) becomes mandatory within 3 months
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## How to apply for permit C in the Canton of Grisons
The process is managed at two levels: cantonal and federal. The canton is the first point of contact; the SEM validates at the national level.
### Phase 1: Document preparation
Before submitting your application, gather: - A valid passport or identity document - A residence certificate from the municipality of current domicile in Switzerland - An extract from the Swiss criminal register (requestable online or at the cantonal police) - Proof of financial stability (employment contract, AVS contribution payments, recent pay slips) - Any cantonal integration certificates (if required by the Canton of Grisons)
The Canton of Grisons specifies the exact list on the migration office website. Some requirements are canton-specific; contact them directly for current details.
### Phase 2: Submission at the Grisons cantonal office
Check the address and opening hours of the migration office (Kantonales Amt für Migration). The application is submitted in person or by registered mail to the office, together with the attachments. Not all cantons accept online applications — check directly before making the trip.
### Phase 3: Transmission to SEM and federal decision
The cantonal office verifies the completeness of the application. If everything is correct, it forwards the file to the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration, based in Bern, Permits Section). The SEM conducts a federal check: criminal record, international data, compliance with migration rules. The decision is sent to the canton, which notifies the applicant of the outcome. Times: on average 2–6 months from submission, depending on cantonal and federal workload.
### Phase 4: Collection and municipal registration
Once approved, permit C is handed over at the cantonal office. It must be registered with the municipality of residence within the indicated deadlines. Registration activates tax and social security rights.
## The path to ordinary naturalisation
Holders of permit C have an open door to ordinary Swiss naturalisation. The federal requirements are: already holding permit C, 10 years of total residence in Switzerland (the last 5 years with permit C count double, therefore reducing the minimum to 5 years with C), no serious criminal record in the last 5 years. In addition, specific municipal and cantonal requirements apply (these vary: some municipalities require knowledge of a national language, additional integration criteria, respect for the cantonal constitution).
The naturalisation application is submitted in two phases: first to the Canton of Grisons, then to the municipality of residence. Each authority has its own deadlines, administrative fees (generally CHF 100–300) and approval procedures.
## Next steps
Use the [Swiss payslip calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate your monthly net pay with federal-cantonal deductions once you have permit C. Check the official Canton of Grisons website for application forms and migration office contact details. If you have children, consider family allowances and cantonal income support benefits. Consult a tax advisor to plan the transition from cross-border worker (if applicable) to ordinary resident, given the significant variation in taxation.

item.title: Naturalization Canton Zug: requirements and complete procedure
item.description: Permit C, 10 years of residence (ages 8-18 count double) and ITER at three levels: municipal, cantonal and federal. Here's how it works in Zug.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Ordinary naturalization in Switzerland requires C permit and 10 years of residence - In the Canton of Zug, specific cantonal and municipal requirements are added - The years of residence between 8 and 18 years old count twice for the purposes of the period - The procedure includes language tests, integration tests and the payment of taxes
## Key facts - **What**: Requirements and procedure for ordinary naturalization in the Canton of Zug - Who: Foreign citizens with residence permit (C) residing in the Canton - Where: Canton of Zug, Switzerland - Federal legal basis: Swiss Citizenship Act (LStr) and related ordinance - Minimum residence: 10 years in Switzerland, with ages between 8 and 18 counting double - Permit required: Permit C (domicile), issued normally after 10 years of residence (5 for EU/EFTA citizens) - Taxation levels: 3 levels (federal + cantonal + municipal DFI), with their own multipliers for each Canton and Municipality
Ordinary naturalisation in the Canton of Zug follows a two-tier process: a federal level, governed by the Swiss Citizenship Act, and a cantonal-communal level, with specific rules of the Canton and the Municipality of residence. To apply you must hold a C permit — the residence permit, which is usually issued in Switzerland after 10 years of residence (5 years for EU or EFTA nationals) — and have at least 10 years of residence in Switzerland. In this The naturalization procedure in the Canton of Zug differs from that of other Cantons due to the bureaucratic speed and clarity of the requirements, elements that also derive from the small size of the Canton. Understanding the practical implications of this process means knowing where the three levels of competence — federal, cantonal and municipal — are located and how they interact.
### Economic and tax implications for the future citizen
Obtaining a Swiss passport brings practical benefits that go beyond the right to vote. From a fiscal point of view, the naturalized citizen is subject to the same IFD + cantonal + municipal regime as any other resident. In Switzerland there is no federal minimum wage (while some cantons — not Zug among those with a mandatory cantonal minimum wage — have their own). The new citizen of Zug will enter a labor market that, for working hours, refers to federal law: maximum 45 hours per week in industry, offices and sales, 50 hours in other sectors; at least 4 weeks of vacation (5 under the age of 20).
On the pension front, naturalisation does not change either the AVS/AHV position or the LPP/BVG situation. The AVS/AI/IPG contributions amount to 5.3% borne by the employee (10.6% total with the employer), AD/AC to 1.1% up to the annual ceiling, LAINF/LAA between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector. LPP/BVG predicts increasing contributions with age
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). Obtaining Swiss citizenship in the Canton of Zug requires a structured process, with precise steps to follow and documents to prepare. The procedure is well-known for being well organized, but it remains articulated across three distinct levels.
### Step-by-step procedure
**1. Check of prerequisites.** First of all, you must ensure that you hold a C permit and have completed at least 10 years of residence in Switzerland (years between age 8 and 18 count double). For EU/EFTA citizens, the C permit can be issued after 5 years of residence according to SEM rules.
2. Document collection. You will need: a valid identity document, C permit, proof of residence, language certificate (German for Zug, at the level required by cantonal law), extract from the Swiss criminal record, certificate of absence of debts (Debt Collection and Bankruptcy Office), proof of financial self-sufficiency, birth certificate and, where applicable, marriage certificate or documents relating to minor children.
3. Municipal application. The first application is submitted to the municipality of residence. Each municipality in the Canton of Zug sets its own additional requirements (years of municipal residence, knowledge of local realities) and its own fee. The municipal council (Gemeinderat) and, in many cases, the municipal assembly (Gemeindeversammlung) or the electorate vote on the granting.
4. Cantonal application. After municipal approval, the application is forwarded to the Migration and Citizenship Office of the Canton of Zug, which verifies cantonal requirements (residence in the canton, integration test, German language, knowledge of cantonal realities). The cantonal fee is paid.
5. Federal application. Once municipal and cantonal approvals have been obtained, the file is forwarded to Bern for the issuance of the federal naturalization authorization. The Confederation checks for the absence of grounds for revocation (serious convictions, dependence on social assistance, etc.) and issues the federal naturalization act.
6. Ceremony and acquisition of Swiss citizenship. Once the process is complete, the applicant obtains the Swiss passport and is registered in the civil status register.
### Where to go and useful tools
For up-to-date information on the specific requirements of the Canton of Zug and your municipality of residence, it is advisable to consult directly the Canton's website (Zuger Verwaltung) and that of the municipality. At the federal level, the reference is SEM (State Secretariat for Migration), which publishes guides and forms. Naturalization fees — federal, cantonal, and municipal — vary in exact amount: it is recommended to request them directly from the relevant offices before starting the procedure.
For those who are dealing with their salary in Switzerland and want to understand the tax impact of their situation — also in view of a change of status — the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) by Frontaliere Ticino is available, useful for simulating net pay and AVS/LPP pension contributions based on the Canton of work.
To get an overview of the overall cost of living in Switzerland — rents, health insurance premiums, taxes — the guide to the [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) offers an updated general picture.
If the goal is to better understand the Swiss tax system before tackling naturalization, the page dedicated to the [tax return](nav:tax-return) can also be a good starting point.

item.title: LAMal Canton Grisons Awards: deductibles and reduction
item.description: Guide to health insurance premiums in the Canton of Graubünden: deductibles from CHF 300 to 2500, alternative models, reduction subsidies and application procedure.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - KVG: compulsory health insurance for Swiss residents - Adult deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2500 (choice of contractor) - Each canton administers premiums and subsidies for reduction
## Key Facts - What: Private health insurance at per capita premiums, not tax - When: Mandatory for residents, stipulated within 3 months of arrival - Where: Single system in all Swiss cantons (including Graubünden) - Who: FSIO/BSV coordinates at federal level; cantons set premiums and subsidies - Amount: Deductibles from CHF 300 (minimum) to CHF 2500 (maximum) for adults
In the canton of Graubünden, as in every Swiss canton, compulsory health insurance (KVG or KVG in German) represents a structural cost for residents. The KVG is not a tax but a private insurance with per capita premiums: each person takes out a free choice of insurer. Premiums vary according to age group, canton (and sometimes region within the canton) and insurance model chosen.
At federal level, FSIO/BSV (Federal Social Insurance Office) coordinates the overall system. However, the cantons independently determine the premiums charged by companies operating in their territory and determine the requirements and amount of subsidies for premium reductions for residents with low incomes.
### Standardised deductibles and cover models
The KVG provides federally standardised deductibles for adults: CHF 300, CHF 500, CHF 1000, CHF 1500, CHF 2000 and CHF 2500. The deductible is the first amount that the insured person incurs out of pocket when seeking outpatient treatment, before the insurance company starts covering the costs. Choosing a higher deductible means paying lower monthly premiums, but taking on more risks in the event of many treatments. Conversely, a low deductible (CHF 300) means higher premiums, but protects against significant unexpected outlays.
In the canton of Graubünden, as in the rest of Switzerland, each insured person evaluates the compromise between monthly premium and protection according to his or her health needs and financial capacity. [Scopri le opzioni di copertura della tua LAMal](nav:health) and compare the available deductibles. ### Alternative insurance models in Graubünden
In addition to the choice of deductible, LAMal offers alternative insurance models that allow the premium to be reduced in exchange for limitations on access to benefits. Among these is the model with a mandatory general practitioner: the contractor enrolls with a trusted doctor and addresses the diagnostic path under his guidance, except for emergencies and certain specialties (ophthalmology, gynecology). Another model is the limited choice insurance of the hospital (network), where access to hospital facilities is restricted to those agreed with the company.
The Canton of Graubünden has particular geographical characteristics — isolated valleys, a population scattered over a vast territory — that influence the offer of alternative models: not all solutions are available everywhere for reasons of territorial accessibility. Check which models are available in your area of Graubünden.
### Cantonal subsidies and premium reductions
Each Swiss canton financially supports low-income residents through subsidies for the reduction of LAMal premiums. The Canton of Graubünden, like the other cantons, provides cantonal funds and federal contributions to reduce the burden for those who cannot afford full premiums. Access criteria and the amount of the reduction vary from canton to canton, as each canton establishes its own income and assets thresholds.

item.title: Buying Zug house: prices, mortgage and costs
item.description: Complete guide to buying real estate in the Canton of Zug: transfer costs, own funds, mortgage loan and cantonal taxes.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Buying a house in Switzerland requires equity capital and an assessment of mortgage affordability. - The transfer tax and notary fees vary by canton and municipality; the Canton of Zug follows its specific cantonal regulations. - Real estate taxation involves three levels: federal (DIT), cantonal and municipal, with different multipliers for each jurisdiction.
## Key facts - **What**: Property purchase in Switzerland through a federal and cantonal administrative procedure - Tax levels: federal DIT + cantonal + municipal (each canton has its own multipliers) - Competences: FTA/ESTV manages the DIT; cantonal administrations manage local taxes - Essential requirement: Equity capital to access bank mortgages - Actors: Notary, banks, Land Registry, cantonal tax offices - Reference rate: SNB sets the national key rate for mortgages
### Three levels of taxation in the purchase process
Buying a house in Switzerland involves a complex interaction between three administrative levels: federal, cantonal and municipal. The taxation burden on real estate transactions reflects this three-pillar structure. At the federal level, the direct federal tax (DIT) applies, which targets the income and capital of property owners. At the cantonal and municipal level, complementary taxes apply to the transfer of real estate ownership.
In the Canton of Zug, as in every Swiss canton, the transfer tax is governed by specific cantonal laws. The cantonal administration sets rates, exemption thresholds and the collection procedure; municipalities can add their own local multiplier. This means that two property purchases of the same economic value, carried out in different cantons, will generate significantly different tax burdens.
The FTA (Federal Tax Administration) and the ESTV (Conference of Cantonal Finance Directors) coordinate the tax system at the national level, but cantonal laws remain sovereign with regard to local taxes. Those buying a house in the Canton of Zug must therefore consult the cantonal tax office to find out exactly the charge applicable to the transfer of ownership in their municipality.
### Equity capital and mortgage access: affordability assessment
A central aspect of buying property in Switzerland is the availability of equity capital and the financial capacity to service the mortgage over time. Swiss banks require a minimum amount of equity capital — defined by each institution's lending policy — before granting a mortgage for the acquisition of a residential property. Mortgage affordability is assessed on the basis of the buyer's income and their ability to make monthly payments over decades. A [salary calculator](nav:calculator) can help estimate the net disposable income and the capacity to service the mortgage.
This assessment process is national — it follows Swiss banking standards and guidelines issued by the Swiss National Bank (SNB) — even though each bank applies its own selection criteria and interest rate pricing. Those intending to acquire a home in the Canton of Zug must therefore present a solid financial plan to local banks, or to institutions elsewhere in Switzerland, to access financing. ### The role of the notary and transfer fees
The transfer of real estate ownership in Switzerland is governed by federal law (Code of Obligations, CO) and by complementary cantonal regulations. The deed of sale — the public transfer document — must be drafted and signed before a notary, whose task is to verify the identity of the parties, the absence of undeclared mortgage debts, and the formal regularity of the contract. Notary fees are borne by the buyer and vary by canton: each canton has its own notary tariffs set by local legislative decrees.
Alongside notary fees, there are administrative charges related to the transfer of ownership rights at the Land Registry office (municipal/cantonal jurisdiction). These amounts also depend on the value of the property and on local regulations. There is no single federal tariff; each canton defines its own collection procedures.
### Mortgage loan and interest rates
The mortgage loan is the main financing instrument for the purchase of residential properties in Switzerland. Once the property has been identified and the required documentation has been collected (pay slips, bank statements, tax returns), the client negotiates the interest rate and the term of the loan with the bank. The Swiss National Bank (SNB) sets the reference rate (key rate) of Swiss monetary policy; mortgage rates follow correlated movements, but each bank applies its own spread and its own commercial policy.
A hypothetical situation: a buyer who has sufficient own funds and a stable income can negotiate a fixed-rate mortgage for 10–20 years. During this period, the mortgage service — the monthly payment of principal and interest — remains constant. Once the term expires, the borrower will need to renegotiate the mortgage or repay the debt using other sources. Contact the [Swiss banks](nav:banks) in the Canton of Zug or in your area to discuss the available financing options and current rates.
### Before signing: energy assessment and technical survey
Before signing the purchase contract, a prudent buyer requests a technical survey of the property to verify its structural condition, plumbing and electrical systems, and other structural risk factors. Moreover, Switzerland has introduced energy efficiency requirements: every building must declare its energy status according to cantonal regulations (which can vary significantly). These checks are not uniformly imposed by federal law, but they are advisable and sometimes required by banks as a condition for financing. The technical survey protects the buyer from hidden renovation costs and allows for a more realistic assessment of the economic sustainability of the investment.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-step procedure for purchasing a property
1. **Search and negotiation**: Identify the property through a real estate agent or online portal, and negotiate the price with the seller. This phase has no federal deadlines — it is purely commercial.
2. Bank pre-qualification: Contact one or more banks and request a mortgage pre-qualification. The bank will verify your income, existing debts, and available own funds, and will communicate the maximum amount that can be financed.
3. Purchase offer: Once the price has been agreed upon, the client or the agent drafts a written offer (sometimes it is a purchase promise subject to various conditions, including financing). The offer defines the price, the delivery date, and any suspensive conditions.
4. Verification of ownership at the Land Registry: Before committing, the buyer (through a notary or agent) verifies that the seller is actually the owner and that there are no hidden mortgages or encumbrances. This is a federal duty of diligence and is registered with the cantonal/municipal Land Registry office.
5. Signing of the deed before the notary: Once the financing has been confirmed by the bank and the documents have been verified, the parties go to the notary to sign the transfer deed. The notary draws up the deed, verifies the identity of the contracting parties, confirms the absence of disputes, and signs the deed.
6. Registration in the Land Registry: Within a short period (variable by canton), the notary files the deed with the competent Land Registry office. The registration legally transfers ownership to the new owner.
7. Mortgage disbursement and payment: After registration in the Registry, the bank disburses the mortgage and pays the seller. From this moment, the buyer is the owner and must begin paying the monthly mortgage.
### Practical tools: where to find information and calculate your purchasing capacity
To assess your payment capacity and the sustainability of the mortgage, it is useful to consult online calculation resources. You can also check information on the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to understand the total impact of the purchase on your overall budget.
Consult the cantonal Land Registry office of Zug for exact notary fees, property transfer tax rates, and the local property registration procedure. Cantonal real estate agencies and notary firms provide up-to-date information on current financing rates and banking conditions.
Finally, it is advisable to consult a notary specialized in real estate law or a cantonal tax advisor to understand exactly what the tax and administrative burdens will be in your specific case.

## Key facts - **What**: Residence permit B (Aufenthaltsbewilligung) in the Canton of Zug - When: Issuance and renewal according to the Federal Law on Foreigners (LStrI) - Where: Canton of Zug, German-speaking Switzerland - Who: Cantonal Office for Migration (Amt für Migration) in Zug, under the supervision of the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) - Requirements: Profit-making activity, adequate accommodation, ascertained identity, sufficient financial means - Duration: Up to 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens; duration linked to the employment contract for third-country nationals - Renewal: Early application before the deadline, verification of conditions, cantonal decision - Documents: Passport, employment contract, accommodation certificate, photos, cantonal forms
The B residence permit in Switzerland is the authorization that allows a foreign national to reside in the country for a period of more than one year, with the possibility of renewal. In the Canton of Zug, the issuance and management of this permit is the responsibility of the Cantonal Office for Migration (Amt für Migration), which operates on the basis of the Federal Law on Foreigners and their Integration (LStrI) and in coordination with the Secretariat of Obtaining the B permit in the Canton of Zug means entering an administrative system that combines federal legislation and cantonal practice. The framework conditions are defined by the LStrI and the ALC, but the methods of submitting the application, the required documentation and the processing times are established at the cantonal level. This creates concrete differences between an applicant who goes to the Zug office compared, for example, to those who go to the similar office of another Canton.
### Practical implications for the applicant
The first practical decision is about timing. The B permit is never automatic: even for EU/EFTA citizens, renewal requires the submission of an application for an extension before the expiry of the licence, accompanied by verification of the original conditions (employment, accommodation, integration) and a new decision by the cantonal authority. Sending the application late may result in the interruption of the right of residence and the obligation to leave the country.
The documentation to be produced typically includes the valid passport, a passport format photo, the employment contract or an employer confirmation, the accommodation attestation (rental contract or owner's certificate), and the specific forms provided by the Cantonal Office of Migration. ### The first step: choosing the legal form
Starting a business in the Canton of Glarus requires first of all the choice of legal form. A limited liability company (Sàrl/SARL) provides minimal capital and offers protection of personal assets, while a public limited company (SA) is suitable for larger structures and attracts external investors.
In the Canton of Glarus, municipalities can apply for registration in the trade register with documents that vary slightly depending on the form chosen. Fill in the tax notification form provided by the financial administration of the Canton of Glarus for company registration. This activates the obligation to file the annual FTA (federal) and cantonal tax returns.

### Operational conclusion
Opening a business in the Canton of Glarus requires structured planning and in-depth knowledge of the Swiss tax, social security, and labour law system. The timings indicated in this checklist are indicative: administrative reality can speed up or delay processes depending on the municipality and the season. However, the overall framework remains valid for any entrepreneur intending to establish themselves legally in Glarus or in any other Swiss canton.
The most important advice is to consult an accountant specialized in corporate law at least when choosing the legal form: initial mistakes create annual administrative complications and lost tax optimization opportunities. Subsequently, delegating the preparation of the annual tax return and accounting management to professionals reduces the risks of non-compliance and maintains smooth relationships with the authorities.
Switzerland is a country with a transparent and well-structured bureaucracy: respecting the deadlines and obligations guarantees smooth operations and regulatory compliance throughout the company's entire life.

item.title: St Gallen Inheritance Tax: Rates and Exemptions
item.description: How inheritance and gift tax works in the Canton of St. Gallen: rates for degree of kinship, exemptions for spouse and descendants, declaration procedure and legal terms.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Each Swiss canton has its own rules on succession and donation - St. Gallen provides exemptions and reduced rates for spouses and children - The declaration must comply with the deadlines set by the canton - The degree of kinship determines the applicable rate
## Key facts - **What**: Cantonal inheritance and gift tax - Where: Canton of St. Gallen (north-eastern Switzerland) - Who: Heirs, beneficiaries, cantonal tax office - Regulatory level: Cantonal law (NOT federal) - Procedure: Declaration with deadlines defined by the canton
In Switzerland, inheritance and gift tax is an exclusively cantonal matter. There is no federal inheritance tax: each canton establishes its own rates, exemptions, procedures and reporting terms. The Canton of St. Gallen applies a taxation system that differentiates the rates according to the degree of kinship between the deceased (or donor) and the heir (or donor).
### Structure of rates by degree of kinship
Sanallian regulations, like those of all Swiss cantons, distinguish between categories of heirs. The spouse, children, and direct descendants generally benefit from significantly lower rates or total exemptions, while brothers, sisters, uncles, cousins, and more distant relatives are subject to progressive and higher rates.
This stepped structure reflects a political choice: to protect the transfer of heritage ## # Switzerland's three-tier tax system
It is essential to understand how inheritance taxation fits into the Swiss federalist structure. Direct taxes operate at three levels: federal (direct federal tax), cantonal and municipal. However, the inheritance tax is entirely cantonal: there is no federal payment or centralized municipal contribution (some cantons, if anything, allow municipalities to apply a supplement).
This total decentralisation generates important disparities between cantons. An inheritance of the same amount can be taxed very differently depending on the canton of residence of the deceased. For example, the Canton of Schwyz does not apply any inheritance tax; the Canton of Geneva also applies rates to children; the Canton of St. Gallen follows an intermediate policy with exemptions for close family members.
## # Living Donations vs. Death Inheritance
An important distinction is between donations (voluntary transfers during life) and successions (death transfers). The Canton of St. Gallen, like most cantons, taxes both cases, although sometimes with different rates.
Donations can benefit from subsidised schemes if they meet certain criteria: for example, donations to charitable, cultural or public benefit organisations often enjoy full or significant exemptions. Donations between parents and children in a straight line
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ### Operational Procedure: Step-by-Step
If you need to deal with an inheritance or a donation in the Canton of St. Gallen, follow these steps:
**Phase 1: Gathering the documentation** Collect the death certificate (for inheritances), the will, the deed of donation (for donations), a complete inventory of assets, property appraisals or valuations, bank statements, ownership documents, and insurance policies. This documentation is essential to correctly complete the declaration.
Phase 2: Identifying the family relationship Precisely determine the degree of kinship between the deceased/donor and the heir/donee (spouse, child, grandchild, sibling, cousin, unrelated person). This data is decisive for applying the correct tax rate.
Phase 3: Contacting the Cantonal Tax Office Immediately contact the Tax Office of the Canton of St. Gallen to: - Obtain the official inheritance tax declaration forms - Receive confirmation of the tax rates applicable to your case - Know the precise filing deadlines - Check whether you benefit from any exemptions or reductions - Clarify any doubts about the valuation of the estate
Phase 4: Completing and submitting the declaration Fill in the official form with all the required information, attach the supporting documents, and submit it within the deadline set by the canton. An incomplete or late declaration exposes you to penalties and interest on arrears.
Phase 5: Receiving the tax assessment notice The Tax Administration will communicate the amount of tax due, which is binding for the taxpayer. You can pay directly or request an instalment payment plan where allowed.
### Critical Deadlines and Legal Time Limits
The deadlines for filing the inheritance tax declaration are set by cantonal law and vary depending on whether it concerns an inheritance (running from the date of death) or a donation (running from the date of signing). It is imperative to check directly with the Cantonal Tax Office what the precise applicable deadline is for your case, as failure to comply results in financial consequences.
An extension can only be requested before the deadline expires and for serious reasons (complexity of the inheritance, need for appraisals, family disputes). The request must be submitted promptly and with proper justification.
### Tools and Resources for Planning
Use our tax calculator to estimate the overall fiscal impact of the inheritance on your situation (also consider the municipal taxes of your municipality of residence). Consult the [guide on the cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living) to understand how the different tax components (federal, cantonal, municipal) are structured in your canton.
### When to Hire a Professional
For complex inheritances, significant estates, family conflicts over wills, or when the family structure is intricate (repeated marriages, children from previous relationships, heirs abroad), turn to a specialised tax advisor or a lawyer experienced in inheritance law. This initial investment often translates into considerable tax savings and an orderly, legally correct management of the estate.
It is advisable to check whether the will or the deed of donation contains provisions relating to the third pillar (3a) or other complementary retirement provision instruments, as these have specific rules regarding taxation and inheritability that differ from ordinary assets.
Contacts and references: - Tax Office of the Canton of St. Gallen (main office and branch offices) - Cantonal associations of Swiss tax advisors - Bar Association of the Canton of St. Gallen for specialists in inheritance law

item.title: LAMal Guide 2026: obligation, cash and deductible
item.description: Compulsory health insurance for those residing in Switzerland: how to enroll in LAMal, choose the cashier and understand deductibles in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Mandatory health insurance for those residing in Switzerland - Three months to register after arrival - Minimum deductible CHF 300 per year, maximum CHF 2,500 - Cantonal subsidies reduce premiums based on income
## Key facts - **What**: Mandatory health insurance (LAMal) - When: Within 3 months of taking up residence in Switzerland - Where: Every canton (including Zurich) has its own premiums and subsidies - Who: All residents of Switzerland, regardless of citizenship - Amount: Deductibles from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 per year
### The LAMal system in Switzerland
Health insurance is one of the cornerstones of Swiss social protection. Unlike many European countries, there is no single national fund: the system is managed by private insurers operating at cantonal and regional level, with premiums that vary significantly from one area to another.
Anyone moving to Switzerland must take out a health insurance contract within three months of arrival. It is neither a tax nor a salary contribution: it is a private premium paid directly to the insurer, calculated on a per-capita basis. This means that each family member pays an individual premium, regardless of the family's income.
### Deductible and coinsurance
The deductible is the amount the patient pays out of pocket before the health fund starts reimbursing. The options vary: CHF 300, CHF 500, CHF 1,000, CHF 1,500, CHF 2,000, CHF 2,500 per year. A higher deductible results in a lower monthly premium; a lower deductible means a higher premium. Once the deductible is reached, the patient shares medical costs (coinsurance) at rates defined by federal law.
The cantonal subsidy reduces the premium for those with low or medium incomes. Each canton, including Zurich, has its own eligibility criteria and subsidy amounts, reflecting local fiscal choices.
### Choosing the right fund
Every canton hosts several health insurers. The choice is not restricted to one specific fund, but the patient must select at least one. Once enrolled, it is possible to switch funds, usually with two or three months' notice at the end of the calendar year. The funds are required to cover the essential services defined by federal law — hospital, general practitioner, medications, tests — but premiums vary widely.
For those residing in the Canton of Zurich, the available funds are numerous. Comparing annual premiums for your age group and deductible type is important, because the difference between two funds can exceed CHF 500–1,000 per year for the same coverage. Several cantons offer online [premium comparison](nav:health) tools to make this choice easier. ## Practical implications: the weight of the premium on the family budget
The choice of the deductible has a direct impact on the annual budget. Those who opt for the minimum deductible (CHF 300) will pay a higher monthly premium than those who choose CHF 2500. For a family with children, this decision is multiplied: three deductibles from CHF 300 cost more than three from CHF 1000, but the initial financial sacrifice is less. The logic is simple: set aside more money each month for more covered insurance, or risk paying more at the time of medical recourse.
### Cantonal subsidy: eligibility and procedure
The premium subsidy is calculated based on your family's net income. In the canton of Zurich, as in the other cantons, eligibility depends on a fixed income threshold that varies annually. Those who are eligible can apply directly to the cantonal authorities, often online. The subsidy is calculated as a percentage of the gross premium and paid directly to the [polizza di assicurazione](nav:health).
Not applying for the subsidy when you are entitled means losing public money intended precisely to cover health costs for those with less ability to pay. Many do not know that the subsidy must be actively applied for — it is not awarded automatically. Applications are usually submitted in the spring, before the deadline of late May or early June, although the exact deadlines vary per canton.
### Comparison between cantons: the same prize
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## How to register for LAMal: the practical steps
Anyone who has just arrived in Switzerland has 3 months to take out a health insurance contract. The procedure is simple but requires prompt action.
### Step-by-step
1. **Gather your documents**: passport/ID, residence permit, cantonal registration certificate of your address (obtainable from the municipal office). 2. Choose a fund: use the cantonal online comparison tools (e.g. the Canton of Zurich portal) to compare premiums for your age and deductible. 3. Fill in the application: the registration form (paper or online) requires personal details, coverage start date, and type of deductible. 4. Pay the first premium: the fund sends an invoice. The first payment must be made within the deadline set by the contract (usually 30 days). 5. Coverage confirmation: the fund issues an insurance card and a coverage document. Only from that moment are you insured.
If you do not take out insurance within 3 months, the cantonal authority can assign you to a fund ex officio (default registration). In that case, you will pay premiums at the full rate with no choice of fund for the following twelve months, and you will have to reimburse any medical costs incurred in the previous 3 months.
### Tools and resources available
Each canton makes available online premium comparison tools (with filters by age, type of coverage, deductible), registration forms (downloadable or digitally fillable), and a cantonal helpline for clarification on subsidies and premiums. In the Canton of Zurich, the official cantonal portal provides access to the comparison tool and up-to-date information. Do not rely on unverified third-party websites: information changes every year and only official portals guarantee accurate data.
### When to change fund: the annual window
The deadline for changing funds is usually 30 November each year, with effect from the following 1 January. Some cantons allow an extraordinary change if the premium increases beyond a certain threshold. Check the specific deadline in your canton, as it varies. Once you have decided to switch, fill in the cancellation form and send it to your current fund (not directly to the new one). Keep the receipt as proof of communication.
The first practical step is to compare premiums in your region according to your personal situation. Use our [LAMal premium calculator](nav:health) to estimate the annual cost based on your age, deductible and canton of residence.

item.title: Neutrality Vote: September 27, Amato Denies Russian Propaganda
item.description: In view of the vote on September 27 on the Neutrality Initiative, Corrado Amato rejects the label of "Russian propaganda" and cites the previous Icelandic of August 29 (52.8% no, 82.5% turnout).
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - Federal vote on September 27 on the Popular Initiative for Neutrality - The author rejects the accusation of “Russian propaganda” leveled at supporters - The Federal Council acknowledges that neutrality safeguards security and prosperity - On August 29, Iceland rejected the reopening of EU accession negotiations
## Key Facts - **What**: Call to defend Swiss neutrality ahead of the September 27 vote - When: Vote scheduled for September 27; reference to the Icelandic vote on August 29 - Where: Switzerland, with a comparison to Iceland - Who: Opinion author: Corrado Amato - Results: Iceland — 52.8% voted “no” to reopening EU negotiations, with an 82.5% voter turnout - Central argument: Neutrality is not isolation, but a tool for security, independence, and prosperity
### An issue concerning the country’s future
Ahead of the September 27 federal vote on the Popular Initiative for Neutrality, supporters of the initiative are sometimes accused of playing into Russian propaganda or of seeking to undermine relations with the West. Corrado Amato rejects this interpretation and calls it a label designed to sidestep the real crux of the debate: “What kind of Switzerland do we want to leave for future generations?”
The fundamental question, the author writes, is simple. Switzerland must continue to be a neutral, independent, and sovereign country, capable of autonomously determining its own foreign and security policy. The point, he adds, is not to choose between Moscow, Washington, or Brussels, but to choose Switzerland: “It is not a matter of being pro-Russian, pro-American, or pro-European. It’s a matter of being pro-Swiss.”
### The Role Recognized by the Federal Council
The author points to a significant political fact: the Federal Council itself recognizes that neutrality safeguards the country’s security, independence, and prosperity. This institutional recognition, according to Amato, makes it even more difficult to justify abandoning this position. Neutrality, he explains, does not mean isolating oneself from the world or renouncing international cooperation: it means being able to engage in dialogue with everyone and, when necessary, offering good offices to promote peace.
In an international context marked by confrontation between major powers, a Switzerland that is “clearly aligned” would risk—as the article argues—losing precisely that role as an independent and credible nation that has historically allowed it to maintain relations with diverse actors. The consequences of this choice, the author warns, will fall most heavily on young people, who will live in a Europe and a world increasingly exposed to geopolitical, economic, and military tensions.
### The Icelandic Precedent
Amato cites a recent example: on August 29, Icelanders rejected, with 52.8% of the vote and an 82.5% turnout, the proposal to reopen negotiations for accession to the European Union. They did not choose—he emphasizes—to shut themselves off from the world, but rather to retain control over their own decisions. It is a message that, in his view, deserves to be heeded in Switzerland as well, where on September 27 there will be an opportunity to reaffirm the principle of a country that is “master of its own destiny.”
Finally, the author warns that reassurances in the moment are not enough: democracy requires evaluating decisions based on their long-term implications, even when someone says, “It won’t happen.” ### What’s Really at Stake on September 27
The popular initiative on neutrality, which will be put to a vote on September 27, touches on one of the historic pillars of Swiss foreign policy. For those who live and work in Switzerland—residents, employees, cross-border workers, and businesses—the issue is not an abstract one, because neutrality shapes the way the Confederation participates in international sanctions, peacekeeping missions, and multilateral economic agreements.
The position expressed in this article is based on a firm conviction: renouncing neutrality would mean subjecting fundamental decisions—on security, foreign policy, and the allocation of resources—to supranational bodies over which Swiss citizens have limited influence. This concern is directly linked to the ongoing debate in Bern regarding the relationship between national sovereignty and European integration.
### The Icelandic Precedent as a Point of Comparison
The Icelandic vote on August 29—52.8% “no” to reopening negotiations with the EU, with an 82.5% turnout—offers a point of comparison explicitly cited by the author. Reykjavík did not choose isolation, but rather democratic control over its own decisions. For Switzerland—a country that is not an EU member but maintains a relationship with Brussels based on a network of bilateral agreements—this parallel raises a question: To what extent is it possible to combine access to the single market with the preservation of decision-making autonomy?
The article also notes that the Federal Council itself recognizes the link between neutrality, security, and prosperity. This institutional recognition reinforces, in the author’s view, the idea that neutrality is not a relic of the past but a foreign policy tool that remains relevant today.
### Implications for Citizens and Businesses
From a practical standpoint, neutrality influences certain concrete aspects of Swiss economic life. International sanctions, for example, are implemented by the Confederation in ways tied specifically to its neutral status. Similarly, participation in European programs related to research, education, or defense depends on the flexibility afforded by neutrality. For exporting companies—many of which operate in the cantons of Zurich, Geneva, Basel, Vaud, and Ticino—the issue also intersects with the broader discussion on competitiveness, the cost of living, and the value of the Swiss franc.
The author does not shy away from issuing a warning: today’s choices will primarily affect future generations. In a Europe rife with geopolitical, economic, and military tensions, Switzerland’s ability to maintain an independent stance is, in his view, a form of protection for the young people who will live through that reality.
### Why the Word “Propaganda” Is Not Enough
Amato challenges the use of the accusation of “Russian propaganda” as a rhetorical shortcut. In his view, reducing the defense of neutrality to a geopolitical label prevents a substantive discussion of an issue that is fundamental to the country. His summary—“pro-Swiss, not pro-Russian”—captures this concern: for the author, defending neutrality means defending Switzerland’s right to decide for itself.
This interpretation fits into a broader context that also touches on the relationship between the Confederation and the cantons. Foreign and security policy decisions fall under federal jurisdiction, yet the repercussions—economic, social, and employment-related—are felt at the cantonal and municipal levels. This is a structural tension that the September 27 vote will not resolve, but which, according to the author, deserves to be at the center of the debate.

## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to find your way ahead of the vote
For a citizen living in Switzerland, September 27 is a date to mark on the calendar. The Popular Initiative on neutrality will be decided at the ballot box: for those eligible to vote, it is time to learn about the text, its practical consequences, and the positions of the main political and economic players.
Corrado Amato's article is not a voting guide, but an opinion piece. However, it contains verifiable elements that are useful for orientation:
- The Federal Council recognises that neutrality safeguards the country's security, independence, and prosperity. - The Icelandic vote of August 29 (52.8% 'no', turnout 82.5%) is cited as a significant precedent. - The debate fits into the broader relationship between national sovereignty and supranational bodies.
### What to do before September 27
A concrete procedure ahead of a federal vote can be outlined in a few steps.
1. Check your registration on the electoral roll. Each Canton manages its own register: it is worth checking in good time that your details are correct, especially after a move or a change of municipality.
2. Read the text of the initiative. The text of the Popular Initiative on neutrality is published on the Confederation's portal and on the Cantons' websites. Reading it directly helps to distinguish between political debate and regulatory content.
3. Consult the official recommendations. The Federal Council and Parliament issue a voting recommendation, available in the federal messages and parliamentary committee reports.
4. Assess the economic implications. For those working in export-oriented sectors, in border Cantons, or in regulated industries, it is worth considering the potential impact on international relations and trade agreements.
5. Go to the polls or vote by post. Procedures vary by Canton: the official envelope, posting deadlines, and polling station opening hours are listed on the website of your Canton of residence.
### Where to find reliable information
The primary sources for information are the Confederation's website (Federal Council message on the initiative, full text), the Cantonal websites (vote explanation, documentation), and the Federal Statistical Office (FSO/BFS) for contextual data on the economy and employment.
For those who want to explore the link between federal political decisions and their wallet, it is also worth keeping an eye on the SNB's monetary policy decisions, which affect the exchange rate and interest rates, as well as SECO data on the labour market.
### A look beyond Switzerland
The article refers to a vote held abroad — the Icelandic one of August 29 — to argue that retaining control over one's own decisions is not the same as isolating oneself. It is an argument that lends itself to comparison with the Swiss debate, where the question of sovereignty returns cyclically, from the 1992 EEA referendum to the discussions on the framework agreement with the EU.
Within this framework, September 27 can be read as one step in a broader debate about the country's direction. Participating in the vote, with an awareness of the text and its consequences, is the most direct tool available to the citizen.
For those who want to simulate the effect of potential economic and fiscal changes on their income, the [Swiss salary calculator](nav:calculator) is a starting point for understanding how national variables — taxes, contributions, exchange rate — affect the payslip.

item.title: Opening business in Nidvaldo: legal forms and costs
item.description: From a sole proprietorship to a corporation (SA): capital, commercial registry, social security contributions, and taxes at three levels for those starting a business in Nidwalden.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Starting a business in Switzerland requires registration with the commercial register - The choice of legal structure determines the minimum capital requirement - Nidwalden: No cantonal minimum wage specified in the source - Registration costs and insurance requirements vary by legal structure
## Key Facts - **What**: Starting a business in the Canton of Nidwalden - When: Current procedure in Switzerland - Where: Canton of Nidwalden - Who: Prospective entrepreneur / founder - Amount: minimum capital based on the chosen legal form - Taxes: taxes at three levels (federal, cantonal, municipal) - Registry: mandatory registration with the commercial registry - Insurance: AVS/AI/IPG, AD, LAINF, LPP in accordance with federal guidelines
Anyone wishing to start a business in the Canton of Nidwalden must navigate a multi-step process that begins with choosing a legal form and continues through registration in the commercial register, opening the necessary bank accounts, and fulfilling tax and insurance obligations. In Switzerland, there is no one-size-fits-all approach: the choice of legal form determines the minimum capital requirement, personal liability, accounting requirements, and recurring costs.
### Legal Forms Available in Switzerland The legal forms permitted by the Swiss Code of Obligations (CO) range from a sole proprietorship—which does not require a minimum paid-in capital but exposes the owner to unlimited personal liability—to a public limited company (SA), including the limited liability company (Sagl). The Sagl requires a minimum capital of CHF 20,000, fully paid in, while the SA requires a minimum capital of CHF 100,000, of which at least CHF 50,000 must be paid in at the time of incorporation. There are also general partnerships, limited partnerships, and cooperatives, each with its own rules regarding capital and liability.
### Registration with the Commercial Register Registration with the Commercial Register is mandatory for corporations (Sagl, SA, general partnerships, limited partnerships, and cooperatives) and optional but recommended for sole proprietorships that exceed certain revenue thresholds. The procedure is handled by the cantonal commercial register office, which in Nidwalden is administered by the canton. The application for registration requires the articles of incorporation authenticated by a notary, the bylaws, the declaration of incorporation, and details of the capital contributions. Registration fees are set at the cantonal level and vary depending on the capital and the complexity of the application.
### Start-up Costs Initial costs include notary fees for the authentication of the articles of incorporation, cantonal fees for registration with the commercial register, and fees for any tax or legal consulting services. Notary fees depend on the capital and the complexity of the articles of association, while registration fees are calculated based on the paid-in capital or, for sole proprietorships, on a fixed cantonal rate. The minimum balance to be deposited into the company’s bank account prior to registration must be documented with a bank confirmation.
### Employer Insurance Obligations A new entrepreneur who hires staff becomes an employer and must enroll in the federal social security programs. AVS/AI/IPG contributions amount to 10.6% of the salary, split 5.3% each between the employee and the employer. AD/AC contributions amount to 1.1% of the salary up to the annual cap. LAINF/LAA premiums range from 0.7% to 1.5% of salary, depending on the sector. For occupational pension plans (LPP), the employee’s minimum contributions on the coordinated portion are 7% (ages 25–34), 10% (ages 35–44), 15% (ages 45–54), and 18% (ages 55 and older up to the reference age). All these amounts follow the federal structure in effect in each canton, including Nidwalden.
### Three-Tier Tax System In Switzerland, taxation operates on three levels: direct federal tax (IFD), regulated in Bern, cantonal tax, and municipal tax. The IFD is calculated in accordance with federal law and is administered by the Federal Tax Administration (AFC/ESTV). Cantonal and municipal taxes are governed by the tax law of the Canton of Nidwalden, which sets the cantonal tax rate; the municipalities then apply their own multiplier. This means that two businesses with identical revenue in different municipalities within Nidwalden may face different tax burdens. VAT is administered at the federal level by the FTA/ESTV itself; businesses with annual revenue exceeding the threshold of CHF 2.5 million must register for VAT and collect the tax on their services. The decision to start a business in the Canton of Nidwalden is not just a matter of initial capital: the practical implications include taxation, social security contributions, mandatory insurance coverage, and retirement planning. Once the legal form has been chosen and registration in the commercial register is complete, the entrepreneur enters a system of recurring obligations that will accompany them throughout the life of the company.
### Tax Implications for the Entrepreneur The first aspect to consider is the distinction between direct federal tax, cantonal tax, and the municipal multiplier. In Nidwalden, each municipality sets its own multiplier, expressed as a percentage of the base cantonal tax. As a result, two companies with identical revenue but located in municipalities with different multipliers pay different amounts of cantonal-municipal tax. Direct federal tax (IFD), on the other hand, follows federal rates, which are uniform throughout Switzerland. Location planning can therefore become a factor in tax optimization, subject to the principle of taxation based on economic capacity.
A second factor concerns the Value-Added Tax (VAT). Businesses whose annual revenue does not exceed the threshold of CHF 2.5 million are exempt from the requirement to register, but may opt for voluntary registration to recover prior-period tax. Above this threshold, registration is mandatory. VAT returns are generally filed quarterly, using rates based on the sector and nature of the service.
### Recurring Personnel Costs If the business involves hiring employees, the employer must manage payroll, which includes: AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% paid by the employee and 5.3% paid by the employer; AD/AC at 1.1% up to the federal annual cap; LPP based on age and coordinated salary; LAINF/LAA with sector-specific premium (0.7–1.5%). The LPP coordinated salary ranges from the entry threshold up to the statutory ceiling, and the minimum contributions indicated above apply only to this range. The minimum LPP contribution rates based on age are mandatory: the employer must pay at least half of the total contributions, as required by the Swiss Code of Obligations (CO) and the LPP.
### Mandatory Health Insurance Self-employed individuals registered in the commercial register and family members working in the business, as well as employees, must take out mandatory health insurance under the LAMal within three months of arriving in Switzerland or starting their business. The LAMal provides for per-capita premiums that are not tied to salary: each resident chooses a deductible of CHF 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, or 2,500. Higher deductibles reduce the monthly premium but expose the insured person to out-of-pocket costs up to the annual maximum. Premiums vary by canton and region; in Nidwalden, the rates of the relevant insurance region apply. The law also provides for premium reductions (cantonal subsidies) for low-income earners, which are paid by the canton of residence.
### Comparison of Legal Structures: A Scenario Let’s consider a business starting with limited capital: a limited liability company (Sagl) requires a capital contribution of CHF 20,000, which must be deposited into a restricted account prior to registration; an SA requires CHF 100,000 in nominal capital, with at least CHF 50,000 paid in. A sole proprietorship has no minimum capital requirement but exposes the owner to unlimited liability: in the event of business debts, personal assets may be seized. For those starting a business with limited risks and low initial investments, a sole proprietorship is the quickest route; for those who intend to bring in partners and limit liability, the Sagl offers the best balance between capital requirements and asset protection. This choice has a direct impact on the tax burden: the profits of an Sagl are taxed at the corporate level (federal income tax + cantonal + municipal), while those of a sole proprietorship are included in the owner’s personal income.
### Relations with Federal and Cantonal Authorities The entrepreneur must interact with several authorities: the FTA/ESTV for federal income tax and VAT, the cantonal authorities of Nidwalden for cantonal and municipal taxes, the cantonal commercial registry office for amendments to the articles of incorporation, and the cantonal offices for AVS/AI/IPG and AD contributions. For occupational pension coverage under the LPP, the employer must join a recognized pension fund. For LAINF/LAA, if the business falls within the mandatory sectors, insurance is administered by SUVA; otherwise, a licensed private insurer is used. Given this multitude of parties to deal with, it is advisable to seek initial consultation covering corporate law, taxation, and labor law.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). After making the decision, an entrepreneur who wants to start a business in Nidwalden must follow a specific procedure. The process can be broken down into distinct steps, each with its own required documents and deadlines.
### Step-by-Step Procedure
**1. Choosing the legal structure.** This decision must be made before taking any other steps. Compare minimum capital requirements, personal liability, accounting requirements, and recurring costs. A sole proprietorship is suitable for low-risk, low-capital businesses; a limited liability company (Sagl) is for those who want to limit liability with an affordable capital requirement; and a corporation (SA) is for projects requiring significant capital and a complex corporate structure.
2. Drafting the articles of association or the memorandum of association. For corporations, a public deed authenticated by a Swiss notary is required. The notary verifies the founders’ identities, collects the incorporation declarations, and prepares the articles of association specifying the capital, purpose, registered office, and organizational structure.
3. Deposit of the minimum capital into a restricted account. For an Sagl, CHF 20,000 must be deposited; for an SA, at least CHF 50,000 (out of a minimum nominal capital of CHF 100,000). The bank issues a deposit confirmation to be attached to the application for registration.
4. Application for registration with the cantonal commercial register. The application must be submitted to the Commercial Register Office of the Canton of Nidwalden, along with the articles of association, the deed of incorporation, the bank confirmation, and the founders’ identification documents. Cantonal registration fees are calculated based on the capital; a flat rate applies to sole proprietorships.
5. Registration for a VAT number with the Federal Tax Administration (FTA). If the projected annual revenue exceeds CHF 2.5 million, or in the case of voluntary opt-in, the company must register for the VAT system with the Federal Tax Administration and begin collecting tax on the services provided.
6. Enrollment in social security and insurance programs. The new employer must register with the cantonal AHV compensation fund, the unemployment insurance (AD) fund, SUVA or the private LAINF insurer for the sector, and a recognized BVG pension fund.
7. Notification to cantonal and municipal tax authorities. The business must be reported to the cantonal tax authority of Nidwalden and to the municipality where the business is located for the taxation of corporate profits (Sagl/SA) or individual income (sole proprietorship).
### Deadlines to Be Met Health insurance under the LAMal must be obtained within three months of the start of business operations or arrival in Switzerland: in the absence of coverage, the authorities will automatically assign you to a plan with a higher premium. The VAT return is filed according to the selected reporting period (typically quarterly) with fixed deadlines set by the AFC/ESTV. AVS/AI/IPG and AD contributions must be paid monthly or quarterly, depending on the agreements with the cantonal fund. LAINF/LAA premiums are generally annual. LPP contributions follow the schedule of the chosen pension fund.
### When to Involve a Consultant The process involves corporate law, tax law, labor law, and social security. A notary is required for the incorporation of a Sagl or SA. For selecting the legal form, optimizing the corporate structure, and establishing relationships with social security agencies, it is helpful to engage an authorized trustee (Treuhaender) who is registered with the cantonal registry. A tax advisor is recommended to set up the accounting system and manage dealings with the AFC/ESTV and the cantonal administration.
For those who wish to simulate the impact of salary and social security contributions on the paychecks of future employees, the [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) tool allows you to estimate net pay and the contributions payable by the employee and the employer based on federal parameters. To assess the gross tax burden on corporate profits and personal income, visit the page dedicated to the tax calculator. For those seeking qualified personnel to hire in Nidwalden or other cantons, the [annunci di lavoro](nav:jobs) section is available.

item.title: Buying a Home in Nidwalden: Prices, Mortgages, and Additional Costs
item.description: Purchase Guide in Canton Nidvaldo: 20% own funds, 33% rule on gross income, transfer taxes and notary fees.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Nidwalden is a Swiss Alpine canton with a residential real estate market - Buying a home requires an assessment of your down payment and mortgage - Transfer taxes and notary fees affect the total cost - Mortgage affordability is calculated based on the 33% rule of gross income
## Key Facts - **What**: Guide to buying a home in the Canton of Nidwalden - Where: Canton of Nidwalden, Central Switzerland - Who: Buyers who are residents or future residents of Switzerland - Topic: Average prices, down payment, mortgage, taxes, and fees - Taxes: 3 levels (federal + cantonal + municipal), with a municipal multiplier - Financing: Down payment generally required to be at least 20% of the property value - Affordability rule: Mortgage payments should not exceed 1/3 of gross income - Purchase restrictions: No restrictions for Swiss citizens; SEM regulations apply to foreign nationals
Purchasing a home in the Canton of Nidwalden follows Swiss federal rules on mortgage financing, supplemented by cantonal tax legislation. Before signing any preliminary agreement, prospective homebuyers must evaluate three aspects: their ability to meet the down payment required by banks, the long-term affordability of the mortgage, and the ancillary costs associated with the transaction.
### The Swiss Tax System Applied to Home Purchases
In Switzerland, taxation occurs at three levels: direct federal tax (IFD), administered by the Federal Tax Administration (AFC/ESTV), cantonal tax, governed by Nidwalden cantonal law; and municipal tax, calculated by applying a municipal multiplier to the cantonal base. Each municipality in Nidwalden sets its own multiplier, which directly affects the owner’s final tax burden. The collection of cantonal and municipal taxes is the responsibility of the cantonal administration, not the federal offices.
Two specific items are then added to the purchase price: the transfer tax (Handänderungssteuer), governed by cantonal tax law, and notary fees regulated by the canton’s notarial legislation. These ancillary costs can significantly impact the overall budget for the transaction.
### Purchase Permit and Residency Requirements
Swiss citizens and holders of a C permit (permanent residence) are free to purchase a home in Nidwalden. For holders of a B permit (residence) and for cross-border commuters with a G permit, however, the restrictions of the Federal Act on the Acquisition of Real Estate by Persons Abroad (Lex Koller) apply, with exceptions for those engaged in gainful employment in Switzerland. The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) is the federal authority responsible for classifying residence permits, while authorization to purchase real estate is the responsibility of the cantonal authorities. ## Mortgage Affordability and Equity
For decades, Swiss banks have applied the so-called “one-third rule”: housing expenses (mortgage, maintenance, and depreciation) must not exceed one-third of the household’s gross annual income. Although this rule is not codified in federal law, it is the market standard and is verified by banks before a mortgage is granted.
### How Much of My Own Funds Do I Need to Contribute?
Banking practice requires that the buyer contribute at least 20% of the property’s value from their own funds, of which 10% must consist of actually available capital (not unredeemed BVG advances). The remaining portion can be covered with funds from the second pillar (LPP) or with a bank loan secured by assets. The LPP (occupational pension plan) is regulated by the Federal Social Insurance Office (UFAS/BSV), which sets the coordinated salary and minimum contributions: 7% for those aged 25 to 34, 10% for those aged 35 to 44, 15% for those aged 45 to 54, and 18% from age 55 up to the reference age.
### Additional Costs: What to Factor In
When calculating your purchase budget, the property price is just the starting point. Notary fees, transfer tax, and land registry registration fees can increase the total cost by approximately 2% to 5% of the sale price, depending on the property’s value and cantonal legislation. In Nidwalden, the transfer tax is governed by cantonal tax law and calculated using specific rates; the revenue from this tax goes to the canton. Notary fees are based on rates established by the canton’s notary legislation.
### Affordability Scenario
A hypothetical buyer with an annual gross household income consistent with the Nidwalden market could obtain a 10-year fixed-rate mortgage and afford the monthly payments according to the “one-third rule.” If interest rates rise, affordability must be reassessed: the Swiss National Bank (SNB) monitors interest rate and mortgage trends as a macroeconomic indicator but does not intervene directly in individual contracts. In case of financial difficulties, options include switching to a variable-rate mortgage, extending the loan term, or selling the property.
### Health Insurance and Cost of Living
Buying a home does not exempt you from the LAMal requirement: mandatory health insurance must be obtained within three months of arriving in Switzerland (for new residents), and premiums vary by canton and region. In Nidwalden, the average premium is indexed annually; deductibles for adults are fixed and range from 300 to 2,500 francs. Premium reductions are administered at the cantonal level.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## The Step-by-Step Process for Purchasing
Before signing a preliminary sales agreement in Nidwalden, it’s helpful to follow a structured process that reduces the risk of unpleasant surprises and optimizes your tax situation.
### Step 1 — Budget Assessment
Calculate your gross household income and apply the one-third rule: mortgage payments, interest, and ancillary costs should not exceed 33% of your gross income. Compare this figure with the price of the property you’re interested in. For a quick estimate of your actual net income, you can use [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator).
### Step 2 — Building Up Your Down Payment
Make sure you have 20% of the purchase price, of which at least 10% should be in cash or liquid assets. If your savings aren’t enough, you can consider a LPP (occupational pension) buyout or a contribution to the third pillar (3a), whose maximum limit is indexed annually. The Federal Social Insurance Office (UFAS/BSV) sets the parameters for the pension pillars, but early withdrawals for a primary residence are subject to specific federal rules.
### Step 3 — Mortgage Application
Gather the documents required by the bank: pay stubs, an extract from the debt enforcement registry, an amortization schedule, and a property appraisal. Compare at least three bank offers: fixed-rate, variable-rate, or LIBOR replaced by SARON; 10-year or 3-year terms. The SNB regularly publishes reference rates, which you can consult to guide your negotiations.
### Step 4 — Preliminary Agreement and Deed of Sale
After signing the preliminary agreement, the cantonal notary reads the deed and drafts the final deed. Notary fees are based on the cantonal fee schedule; the transfer tax is calculated based on the sale price in accordance with the canton’s tax law.
### Step 5 — Registration in the Land Registry
The registration of ownership in the Nidwalden Land Registry completes the process. From that moment on, you are the full owner.
### Step 6 — Post-Purchase Tax Return
After the purchase, update your cantonal and federal tax returns: mortgage interest is deductible from taxable income, according to federal, cantonal, and municipal tax rates. For the [dichiarazione delle imposte](nav:tax-return) form, please refer to the instructions provided by the cantonal administration.
