item.title: The Swiss army focuses on drones: the 2026 strategy
item.description: New drone center of excellence, battalion, and recruit school starting in 2028. Expert Gilli: the right direction, with limitations on scale and rapid innovation cycles.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance
- Swiss Army: New drone center of excellence and specialized battalion - Drone recruit school starting in 2028; funding in the policy phase - Expert Gilli (Hertie School): The right direction, but with limitations in scale - Switzerland ahead of Austria; AI and high-power lasers among the advantages
## Key Facts
- **What**: Swiss Army focuses on drones with a new center of excellence, battalion, and recruit school - When: Recruit school starting in 2028; analysis in August 2026 - Where: Switzerland; technological research in Zurich and Lausanne - Who: DDPS, analyst Mauro Gilli (Hertie School Berlin) - Context: The war in Ukraine has lasted nearly 5 years; military strategies have been transformed - Funding: Under discussion at the federal level - Comparison: Switzerland is further ahead than Austria in its preparations
### The Army’s Modernization Efforts and Drone Strategy
The Swiss Army is accelerating its pace toward technological modernization. On the ground, this involves the launch of a new center of excellence dedicated to unmanned aerial vehicles, and on the political front, it includes debates on the funding of these new capabilities. The initiative includes a new specialized battalion and a recruit school set to open in 2028—a sign of medium-term strategic investment in a sector that the war in Ukraine, now in its nearly fifth year, has made central to modern operations.
But is what Switzerland is doing enough, compared to neighboring powers? Mauro Gilli, professor of military strategy and technology at the Hertie School in Berlin, spoke to SEIDISERA about this. The direction Switzerland is taking is the same as that of the vast majority of Western countries, Gilli explains. It involves seeking greater automation and greater reliance on emerging modern technologies, such as drones. However, whether this is sufficient or adequate for modern needs remains very difficult to say for any country. These are precisely the lessons learned from military conflicts.
### Is Switzerland Ahead of Its Neighbors? A Comparison with Austria and Germany
When discussing the adequacy of defense, comparisons with neighboring countries become inevitable. But not all comparisons are appropriate. Germany, due to its size and the role it plays in Europe and NATO, faces different threats than France and Italy, and finds itself in a situation completely different from all the others, Gilli points out.
For Switzerland, the most sensible comparison is with Austria. And from this perspective, the available data suggests a Swiss advantage: based on the information available, Switzerland appears to be further ahead in the development and adoption of drone systems. ### The Advantages and Limitations of the Swiss Supply Chain
A nation’s ability to equip itself with drones and defense technologies depends not only on strategic intentions but also on industrial realities. A study recently published by Gilli’s former colleagues at ETH Zurich shed light on this very aspect.
According to the study, Switzerland enjoys “significant advantages due to the fact that it is a highly technologically advanced country with a sophisticated industrial base across multiple sectors.” However, there is a flip side to the coin. “There is a problem of scale. In practice, it is very difficult to have the capacity to produce all these components or to procure all the necessary materials in the required quantities,” explains Gilli. [Le aziende svizzere leader nel settore aerospaziale e tecnologico si confrontano quotidianamente con questa sfida di scalabilità](nav:companies).
The problem is further complicated by the accelerated product cycle of modern warfare. Drones, which are state-of-the-art today, can become obsolete within a matter of months. “Within a few months, drones can go from being the most advanced technology to being obsolete, precisely because the adversary has developed countermeasures.” This continuous acceleration of the cycle of measures and countermeasures makes it difficult to maintain a stable technological advantage.
### Lack of Consensus Among Experts: Caution vs. Massive Innovation
Contrary to what is sometimes claimed, there is no universal agreement that drones should be the top priority for future military investments. No, there is no consensus—that much is clear. On the one hand, some analysts and experts advocate for a more widespread adoption of these new technologies. On the other hand, there are other analysts, experts, and commentators who suggest greater caution.
And why is that? The history of warfare is a history marked by a continuous cycle of measures and countermeasures. Military revolutions are not all that frequent. This divergence of opinion among experts serves as a reminder that military investment decisions remain complex and subject to differing assessments, even within the community of military strategists and technologists. There is therefore no single, unambiguous position that favors drones as the definitive solution.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Drone Defense: AI and High-Power Lasers as Swiss Keys
While drone attacks have become a central concern, the ability to defend against them is equally critical. On this front, publicly available information is very limited, Gilli admits. But this is precisely where one of Switzerland’s strengths lies.
The country—and in particular cities like Zurich and Lausanne—boasts world-class scientific and technological research centers. These universities and institutes have developed a highly advanced technological and industrial base in precisely those sectors that are key to neutralizing drones. Which sectors? First, artificial intelligence, which is key to identifying, detecting, and recognizing enemy drones. Second, other more physical technologies such as high-powered lasers that cause mechanical problems for drones by heating them up. These research and development capabilities position Switzerland not only as an importer of technology but also as a potential producer of defense solutions.
### Implications for the Swiss Research and Technology Sector
The Swiss Army’s plan to develop new in-house expertise in drones has broader implications. It means investing in national research in critical sectors (AI, sensor technology, defense materials), which in turn could generate skilled jobs at Swiss centers of excellence. The 2028 deadline for launching the drone recruit school signals a concrete medium-term commitment. It is a sign of both strategic ambition and the need to train in-house personnel capable of operating and maintaining these systems.
For those interested in careers in the defense, research, and technological innovation sectors in Switzerland, this represents a concrete window of opportunity. The AI and advanced technology research centers in Zurich and Lausanne offer growing career prospects.
### What to Expect in the Coming Months
Funding for the drone development strategy remains in the political phase. This means that the federal debate over the resources to be allocated will continue. In the meantime, the military will continue its operational preparations. The central question remains: How much should we invest today in a technology that could become obsolete tomorrow? For Switzerland, the answer seems to be finding a balance: making informed strategic choices and leveraging the advantages of its technological and industrial base, but without deluding itself that drones are the ultimate military solution. ## Key Facts - **What**: Home purchase and related tax procedures - When: Notarized signing and tax payment within the first tax year - Where: Cantonal notary’s office, banks, tax office - Who: Notary, lending institution, cantonal tax office - Tax levels: Federal, cantonal, and municipal for each transaction
Buying a home in the Canton of Nidwalden involves a significant investment subject to specific Swiss regulations. The process of purchasing real estate follows a defined path, with mandatory involvement of notaries and taxes determined by the three-tier tax system: federal, cantonal, and municipal.
### The Notary’s Role in the Process In Switzerland, signing a real estate purchase deed requires the involvement of a notary, a professional regulated by federal law. The notary verifies ownership of the property, drafts the deed of sale, and oversees its registration in the canton’s land registry. This role is essential to ensure the legality and traceability of the property transfer. Without notarial involvement, the transfer is not valid.
### The Swiss Tax System and Housing Property taxation in Switzerland operates on three levels. The Confederation collects direct federal tax on income from real estate (rental income and capital gains). The cantons and municipalities set their own property and inheritance tax rates, which are applied locally. In the Canton of Nidwalden, as in every other canton, cantonal regulations determine specific taxes on property transfers. This three-tiered structure is unique to the Swiss system and varies significantly among cantons and municipalities.
### Timing of the Transfer Tax The property transfer tax is collected at the time of the property transfer, which is usually handled by the notary when the deed is signed. It falls under cantonal jurisdiction; therefore, the rate and collection procedures follow the specific laws of the Canton of Nidwalden. Payment is made during the notarial procedure and must be completed to finalize the property registration. Each canton has its own criteria for calculating and applying this tax, with significant differences based on the property’s price and the degree of kinship between the parties. ### Transfer Tax: Cantonal Variations The transfer tax is an exclusively cantonal matter in Switzerland. This means that each canton has its own laws regarding the tax rate, exemptions, and calculation methods. In the canton of Nidwalden, as in Schwyz, Uri, and Glarus, the rates and criteria may differ significantly from those in cantons such as Zurich, Geneva, or Basel. Some cantons apply progressive rates based on the property’s price or the degree of kinship between the seller and buyer. Family purchases may qualify for significant tax breaks. Comparing transfer tax rates among neighboring cantons reveals just how much this tax affects the final cost of the purchase.
### Notary Fees and Incidental Costs In addition to the transfer tax, the purchase of a property involves notary and administrative fees. These include the notary’s fees (calculated based on the property’s value), land registry fees, stamp duties, and property appraisal costs required by the financing bank. In the Canton of Nidwalden, these costs are governed by the cantonal notary law, which establishes fees and calculation methods. The total expenses represent a significant percentage of the purchase price. It is advisable to request a detailed estimate from the notary before proceeding.
### Mortgage Affordability: Bank Criteria The ability to obtain a mortgage and its affordability depend on criteria defined by Swiss banks. Banks generally evaluate the ratio between the requested loan amount and the property’s value, the household income available for repayment, the applicant’s employment status, and their credit score. Most banks require a down payment, the amount of which varies by institution and the customer’s profile. Personalized banking advice is essential to understanding your financing options and your actual chances of securing a loan.
### Comparison of Purchase Scenarios To understand the total costs of a home purchase, it is helpful to examine hypothetical scenarios. Imagine a buyer who intends to purchase a property in the canton of Nidwalden. The negotiated price, available equity, the requested mortgage, the applicable transfer tax (determined by cantonal law), and notary and registration fees, when combined, provide an estimate of the total costs. When comparing the same transaction in a neighboring canton, differences in tax and administrative costs become apparent, highlighting the importance of also considering taxation when choosing where to buy. Online tools and calculators can help estimate these costs based on the specific situation.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Step-by-Step Procedure The process of purchasing a home in Switzerland follows a specific sequence. The first step is to search for a property and negotiate the price with the seller. Once an agreement is reached, the parties sign a preliminary purchase agreement, a legally binding document that formalizes the intention to buy. Next, the buyer requests an appraisal of the property and submits a mortgage application to the bank. The bank approves the loan based on the appraisal and the applicant’s profile. Once approval is granted, the parties go to the notary’s office to sign the final deed. The notary verifies the documentation, records the transfer in the land registry, and collects the transfer tax. Finally, the notary transfers the funds to the seller, and the buyer becomes the legal owner.
### Checklist of Essential Documents Before proceeding, make sure you have the necessary documentation on hand: current title certificate (land registry extract), identification document, proof of income (tax returns or pay stubs for the last 2–3 years), employment contract, and a certificate of good conduct (if required by the bank). A professional property appraisal is essential, as the bank will use it to determine the maximum loan amount. All of these documents help speed up the process and reduce the time it takes to approve the mortgage. Prepare the documents in advance and check with the bank to see if any other specific documents are required.
### Approximate Timeline for the Purchase From the initial offer to the closing of the transaction, the process typically takes 2–4 months, depending on the complexity of the transaction and the bank’s processing speed. It usually takes 1–2 weeks from signing the purchase agreement to submitting the mortgage application. Mortgage approval takes 2–4 weeks on average. From approval to notarization, the time depends on the notary’s availability and the accuracy of the documentation—generally 1–2 weeks. Overall, once the property has been identified, the entire transfer process requires patience and coordination among the bank, the notary, and the seller.
### Next Steps If you’re considering purchasing a property in the Canton of Nidwalden, the first step is to contact local banks for preliminary advice on financing criteria and mortgage pre-approval. Next, consult a notary public registered in the canton for advice on transfer taxes and specific administrative fees. A real estate advisor can guide you in finding properties that fit your budget. Finally, use online tools and calculators to estimate tax amounts based on your specific situation. [nav:calculator] Use our calculator to estimate taxes and fees for your home purchase.

## In a nutshell - Buying a house in Canton Nidvaldo: niche market, prices below the national average - Own funds required: at least 20% of the purchase price for the mortgage loan - 10% of the funds must be 'actually available', not from social security - Ancillary expenses: transfer tax, notary fees and registration in the land register
## Key facts - **What**: Practical guide to buying a house in the Canton of Nidvaldo - When: Current baseline scenario for 2026 - Where: Canton of Nidvaldo (Obvaldo and central Switzerland) - Who: Private buyers resident in Switzerland - Amount: Minimum own funds not yet specified in the source - Reference: Mortgage financing governed by federal and cantonal legislation - Cost items: Transfer tax, notary fees, land registry fees - Documents: Preliminary contract, registration in the Land Registry, notarial deed
### Average prices and real estate market in Nidvaldo
Canton Nidvaldo is among the smallest cantons in the Confederation and its real estate market reflects this dimension. Average homeownership prices (single-family homes and flat properties) tend to be below the Swiss national average, although the difference has narrowed in recent years. Demand comes largely from residents of the canton itself and from buyers from the neighbouring cantons of central Switzerland.
For those who evaluate the purchase, ### Analysis: How Affordable Is It to Buy a Home in Nidwalden?
Nidwalden offers an attractive option for those seeking a balance between purchase price and quality of life. The entry-level price for a home is generally lower than in the cantons of Zurich, Geneva, or Basel-Stadt, but the gap has narrowed. Mortgage affordability depends on three factors: mortgageable income, equity, and the mortgage interest rate.
The 35% rule is the prudential benchmark used by financial institutions: housing expenses (mortgage interest, principal payments, and maintenance) should not exceed about one-third of gross income. This criterion, which is not codified in federal law but is applied by banks, effectively sets the ceiling on the mortgage amount that can be granted.
### Hypothetical Comparison: Three Financing Scenarios
Scenario A — Purchase with substantial down payment: A household with 35–40% of the purchase price available as a down payment qualifies for a loan with an LTV of 60–65%, resulting in more favorable interest rates and lower monthly payments.
Scenario B — Purchase with minimal down payment: Those who have only the required 20% must optimize the mandatory unrestricted portion (10%) by drawing on liquid savings, while the remaining 10% can come from a BVG advance or a 3a withdrawal.
Scenario C — Under-sized Purchase: Those who do not reach 20% equity will not obtain bank financing. The LPP and 3a accounts can bridge the gap only up to 10% of the purchase price.
### Effects on Retirement Savings
Transferring capital from the LPP or 3a to a real estate purchase has direct effects on future retirement benefits. An LPP advance reduces the capital accumulated with the pension provider and thus the AVS/AHV pension supplemented by the second pillar. Withdrawals from the 3a pillar are taxed as income unless reinvested in a home within the time limits set by federal law (LPP). The UFAS/BSV is the federal agency responsible for social security (AVS, AI, LPP), but it does not set tax rates: taxation on 3a withdrawals falls under the jurisdiction of the Federal Tax Administration (IFD) and cantonal tax authorities.
### Cost of Living and Recurring Expenses
The cost of living in Switzerland is structurally high, and Nidwalden is no exception: premiums for mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) vary by canton and region, and every resident must enroll in LAMal within three months of arrival or birth. Deductibles for adults are set at the federal level (CHF 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, or 2,500). The cantons administer premium reductions for low-income households. The LAMal is a private, per-capita premium-based system; it is not a payroll tax.
The Confederation schedules four referendums per year on federal issues: any constitutional amendments require a double majority of the people and the cantons. For those considering a long-term real estate purchase, federal policies regarding the AVS, LPP, and mortgage amortization are important contextual factors.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Concrete procedure: buying a house in Nidwalden
The purchase of a home in Switzerland follows a sequence of steps standardized at the federal level (law of obligations, CO), with cantonal elements specific to Nidwalden. Here are the operational steps.
### Step 1: Financial verification and own funds
Before searching, the potential buyer gathers the documents needed for the bank check: last three pay slips, pension fund statement, pillar 3a statement, asset certificate and table of outstanding debts. The bank calculates the mortgageable income and the maximum mortgage it can grant by applying the 35% rule on housing costs. For employees with a permanent contract, the mortgageable income is generally based on the gross salary.
### Step 2: Search, offer and preliminary contract
The property search takes place through Swiss real estate portals and local agencies. Once the offer is accepted, a preliminary contract (Reservierungsvertrag or Kaufvertrag) is signed with payment of a confirmation deposit. The notary is involved at this stage to draw up the public deed.
### Step 3: Notarial deed and registration in the Land Register
The public deed of sale is drawn up by a notary authorized in Nidwalden. Notary fees follow Nidwalden cantonal tariffs. Registration in the Land Register (Grundbuch) is mandatory for the transfer of ownership: without registration, the buyer does not become the owner in full effect.
### Step 4: Payment of the price and taxes
Payment of the price takes place through a blocked account or fiduciary deposit. The real estate transfer tax is due on the deed of sale and follows the rate and exemptions provided for by Nidwalden cantonal legislation. Specific exemptions are provided for in Nidwalden for certain transfers, for example between spouses or in the event of inheritance.
### Step 5: Recurring costs after purchase
After the purchase, the home generates recurring costs: wealth taxes (federal direct tax, cantonal and municipal taxes), LAMal premium per household, SUVA premiums if self-employed, municipal waste disposal fee. The municipal multiplier in Nidwalden applies to the cantonal tax and varies by municipality.

To plan your post-purchase budget, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the impact of social contributions and direct tax on net income. To compare purchasing power with the border area, the [currency exchange comparator](nav:exchange) CHF/EUR is updated daily. To estimate the annual LAMal burden, consult the [health insurance guide](nav:health) with average premiums by canton.

## At a Glance - Nidwalden: A residential market with dynamics distinct from the national average - Buying a home: Financial planning and documents to prepare carefully - Mortgage: Equity requirement and affordability assessment - Additional costs: Transfer taxes and notary fees to factor into your budget
## Key Facts - **What**: A practical guide to buying a home in the Canton of Nidwalden - When: current context; to be reviewed annually - Where: Canton of Nidwalden, Swiss Confederation - Who: private buyers intending to purchase a property for residential purposes - Amount: varies depending on the property price and financing
Buying a home in the Canton of Nidwalden requires careful preparation, because while Switzerland has a uniform federal framework for certain matters—such as property law and the tripartite tax structure—it grants the cantons broad autonomy regarding tax rates, building codes, and municipal procedures. For a buyer entering the Nidwalden real estate market for the first time, it is helpful to immediately distinguish between three levels of regulation: federal law (the Swiss Code of Obligations governing sales, real property law), Nidwalden cantonal legislation, and the regulations of individual municipalities, which may impose specific requirements or conditions.
The first concrete step is assessing financial feasibility. Before signing a preliminary agreement, the buyer should form a realistic idea of the market price in the chosen region—by comparing listings, data published by the Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS), and information provided by banks and brokers—and, at the same time, verify their ability to take on debt with a sustainable mortgage. There is no federal minimum wage in Switzerland, so income assessment is based on actual salary, while the ratio of mortgage payment to income remains the key criterion.
### Documents and Seller Verification The preliminary phase involves analyzing the land registry extract, identifying any easements, encumbrances, and rights of first refusal, as well as verifying the property’s mortgage status. A technical inspection of the property is recommended to identify defects that could affect the price or require investments in the months following the purchase. Nidwalden, like the rest of Switzerland, does not mandate a single appraisal model, but banks granting mortgage loans generally require a professional appraisal to determine the property’s loan-to-value ratio.
The article continues with an analysis of ancillary costs and taxes, as well as the financing options available on the Swiss market. ## Purchase Costs and Applicable Taxes
In Switzerland, real estate taxes consist of several components that the buyer must factor in alongside the purchase price. Property transfer tax is regulated at the cantonal level: each canton applies its own tax rate and rules, so it is necessary to consult the Nidwalden cantonal tax authority to determine the exact amount due at the time of transfer of ownership. In addition, there are notary fees—which also vary depending on the notary’s fee schedule and the complexity of the transaction—as well as costs for registration in the land registry.
At the federal level, it is important to note that the Confederation does not impose a specific tax on the transfer of residential real estate: the Swiss tax system is based on the federal direct tax (IFD), the cantonal tax, and the municipal tax. The authority to set cantonal and municipal tax rates lies with the cantonal administrations and municipalities, never with the FTA/ESTV, which deals exclusively with the Federal Direct Tax (FDT) and VAT. It is therefore pointless to contact the ESTV for clarification on Nidwalden’s transfer tax; instead, you should consult the relevant cantonal office directly. The Federal Social Insurance Office (UFAS/BSV) and the SNB have no jurisdiction over real estate taxation.
### Down Payment and Mortgage Affordability The key issue for buyers in Nidwalden remains the equity requirement set by the Swiss banking system. Although there is no single federal regulation on this matter, established practice requires that the buyer have a substantial amount of equity relative to the property’s value. A portion of these funds may come from occupational pension plans (LPP/BVG) through an early withdrawal for a primary residence, or from Pillar 3a. The specific conditions for accessing these options are governed by federal pension legislation and cantonal regulations.
To assess affordability, the buyer must compare the projected mortgage payment with their income, while also taking into account the property’s ongoing costs (maintenance, LAMal/KVG premiums if they already have mandatory health insurance, and ancillary expenses). The prudential model adopted by the Swiss banking sector assesses the ability to service the mortgage not only at the current interest rate but also under scenarios involving higher rates. When determining the calculation rate, it is advisable to inquire with financial institutions about the assumptions they use.
### Comparing Financing Options Various types of mortgages are available on the market: fixed-rate, variable-rate (SARON), and hybrid. The choice depends on how long you plan to stay in the home and your personal risk tolerance. Comparing offers from multiple banks remains the most effective strategy for securing favorable terms, especially since the banking sector in Switzerland is highly competitive.
A second practical consideration involves recurring costs after the purchase: the periodic taxation of property value (property tax), premiums for mandatory fire insurance, and health insurance premiums under the LAMal/KVG—which are private, calculated on a per-capita basis, and do not constitute a payroll contribution, with cantonal premium reductions available for low-income earners. Although not all of these elements can be precisely quantified at the source, they must be included in the overall financial planning.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Purchase Process
Buying a home in Nidwalden follows a series of standardized steps that the buyer can manage independently or with the assistance of a consultant. A typical process consists of seven steps.
### Step 1 — Financial Self-Assessment Before contacting banks or sellers, the buyer gathers personal documentation (pay stubs, statements from the three pension pillars, and any other sources of income) and sets a rough budget. The [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) tool allows you to simulate the impact of the mortgage payment on your monthly net income.
### Step 2 — Property Selection and Viewing Once one or more properties of interest have been identified, the buyer conducts on-site visits and gathers information on the building’s condition, condominium fees (if it is a condominium), and local zoning regulations.
### Step 3 — Mortgage Application With the documentation gathered, the buyer submits mortgage applications to two or three banks. The banks assess the feasibility of the loan based on income, the property’s value, and the amount of available equity.
### Step 4 — Preliminary Agreement and Deposit After an agreement on the sale is reached, the parties sign a preliminary agreement and pay a confirmatory deposit. The amount of the deposit and the conditions for withdrawal are negotiated between the parties.
### Step 5 — Preparation of the Notarial File The notary verifies the documentation, prepares the public deed of sale, and coordinates the registration in the land registry. The notary’s fees are regulated at the cantonal level.
### Step 6 — Payment of the Purchase Price and Transfer of Possession On the agreed-upon date, the buyer pays the balance of the purchase price through the notary’s escrow account and receives the keys to the property. At the same time, the cantonal property transfer tax and registration fees are paid.
### Step 7 — Insurance and Administration After the purchase, it is advisable to update the mandatory fire insurance coverage and, if applicable, update your LAMal/KVG health insurance information using the [guida salute](nav:health) form on the website. For salaried employees, AVS/AHV and LPP/BVG contributions continue to be withheld at source by the employer according to the current federal rates (AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% paid by the employee, with the employer paying a total of 10.6%).
To best prepare for your paycheck after taking out a mortgage, it is helpful to consult the [comparatore busta paga](nav:payslip) form and simulate the deductions using the tax calculator. If the purchase involves a transition from tenant to homeowner, please note that the rules governing tenancy (Art. 253 et seq. of the Swiss Code of Obligations (CO), referred to in the source as federal law) no longer apply to the new situation. For a comprehensive assessment of [costo della vita](nav:cost-of-living) in Switzerland after the purchase, the website provides tools dedicated to analyzing the family budget.
For those wishing to learn more about cantonal real estate taxation, the starting point remains the Nidwalden tax administration, the only reliable source for current tax rates and local tax breaks.

### The Federal Framework
The Swiss tax system is organized into three distinct levels: direct federal income tax (IFD), cantonal tax, and municipal tax. The IFD and VAT fall under the jurisdiction of the Federal Tax Administration (AFC/ESTV), while cantonal and municipal taxes are the responsibility of the cantonal administrations. Each canton has its own tax law and tax multiplier; municipalities apply an additional multiplier to the cantonal tax. The Federal Social Insurance Office (UFAS/BSV) administers social security (AVS, AI, LPP) but does not set taxes, and the Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) produces data without influencing tax rates.
### Labor Costs for Employees
Wages are subject to contributions that affect the savings capacity needed to purchase a first home. AVS/AI/IPG account for 5.3% paid by the employee (10.6% total including the employer’s share), AD/AC for 1.1% up to the annual cap, and LAINF/LAA between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector. BVG contributions on the coordinated salary vary by age group: 7% (ages 25–34), 10% (ages 35–44), 15% (ages 45–54), and 18% (ages 55 through the reference age). Mandatory health insurance (LAMal) is a private per-capita premium, not a payroll contribution, and must be taken out within three months of arrival in Switzerland. The standard deductibles for adults are CHF 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000, or 2,500.
### The National Housing Context
Federal law governing leases (Art. 253 et seq. CO) applies uniformly across all cantons: a maximum security deposit equal to three months’ rent, held in a restricted account in the tenant’s name; a landlord’s notice of termination is valid only if submitted on an official cantonal form; and a dispute must be filed with the conciliation authority within thirty days. The contractual framework for employment provides for maximum weekly working hours of 45 hours (manufacturing, offices, retail) or 50 hours for other sectors, a minimum of four weeks of vacation (five weeks for those under 20), fourteen weeks of maternity leave at 80% pay (IPG) and two weeks of paternity leave. There is no federal minimum wage, but some cantons have their own. Notice periods are one, two, or three months during the first year, the second through ninth years, and the tenth year and beyond, respectively. ### The three income taxes and their impact on the household budget
A buyer in Canton Nidvaldo must consider that the income tax levy follows the three-tier model already mentioned. The federal direct tax (IFD) is fixed by the Confederation and applied by the AFC/ESTV, but the preponderant part of the personal tax burden derives from the cantonal and municipal tax, with locally established rates and multipliers. The municipal multiplier is applied to the cantonal tax and can also vary significantly between neighbouring municipalities. This means that two families with identical income, residing in different municipalities of the Canton, can bear significantly different tax burdens — an element that affects the long-term sustainability of the mortgage.
## # Actual Savings Capacity
Between deductions for social contributions and taxes, net disposable income is significantly reduced compared to gross. An employee must consider that the AVS/AI/IPG and LPP contributions directly reduce the paycheck, while the federal, cantonal and municipal tax is levied retrospectively on the tax return. For those planning to purchase a property, the ability to accumulate the necessary own funds within a realistic horizon depends precisely on the monthly net balance, not on gross income. It is this balance that determines the rate at which the initial capital can be set aside, taking into account
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-Step Guide for First-Time Homebuyers
Anyone considering the purchase of a home in the Canton of Nidwalden can follow a process divided into several stages. The first step is to assess long-term financial sustainability by simulating the impact of interest, principal payments, and ancillary costs on the household budget. The second step involves gathering income documentation (pay stubs, salary certificates, and tax returns from recent years) to submit a loan application to financial institutions. The third step involves consulting the land registry to verify that there are no mortgages or encumbrances on the selected property.
### Documents and Administrative Requirements
Purchasing real estate in Switzerland requires the services of a notary to draft the public deed of sale and register the transaction in the land registry. Notary fees and the transfer tax (Handänderungssteuer) are set at the cantonal and municipal levels. For residents, taking out mandatory health insurance (LAMal) is a prerequisite from the moment they arrive in Switzerland, with a three-month deadline for selecting an insurer. For foreign nationals, the relevant residence status (B or C permit, or G permit for cross-border commuters) affects the ability to purchase residential real estate, a matter governed by the Federal Act on the Acquisition of Real Estate by Persons Abroad (LIAFE).
### Tax Deadlines and Requirements
Once the property has been purchased, the new owner must consider the deductibility of mortgage interest and depreciation on their cantonal and federal tax returns, in accordance with the rules applicable in their canton of residence. The tax return follows the cantonal schedule, generally due in the spring of the following year. For employees, the obligation to pay AVS/AI/IPG contributions begins automatically upon employment, while LPP contributions are withheld by the employer based on the employee’s age bracket. Direct federal tax is calculated based on the annual tax return, which must be filed with the relevant cantonal tax authority.
### Useful Tools for Orientation
To simulate the impact of a mortgage on your take-home pay and overall tax burden, it’s helpful to start with [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator). To compare the cost of living across cantons and assess the effect of health insurance premiums on your family budget, [tool costo della vita](nav:cost-of-living) offers a starting point. For those who wish to plan additional contributions to Pillar 3a and thereby reduce their tax burden, the guide to [terzo pilastro](nav:pillar3) clarifies the deductible limits and withdrawal conditions. For a decision of this magnitude, it remains essential to compare multiple bank offers and seek independent mortgage advice before signing the contract.

## In a nutshell - St. Gallen: diversified economy between industry, services and trade - No federal minimum wage in Switzerland - Sector CCL with or without general obligation - Salaries related to training, experience and level of responsibility
## Key facts - **What**: Structure of the labour market in the Canton of St. Gallen - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, eastern Switzerland - Who: Employers, employees, State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), Federal Statistical Office (FSO/BFS) - When: Current context, with annual updates - Amount: No federal statutory minimum wage; CCL-determined wages, individual contracts, and level of training
The labour market in the Canton of St. Gallen reflects the economic structure of eastern Switzerland: a diverse productive fabric, where manufacturing, financial and insurance services, trade, health and training coexist. Those looking for work or who want to understand how their salary is positioned must consider three fundamental variables: the sector of activity, the degree of training and the experience gained.
### Sectors hiring
In St. Gallen, as in the rest of Switzerland, the demand for labour is concentrated in the sectors of services, health, mechanical engineering and technology. The cantonal economy benefits from the proximity to the economic poles of Zurich and the Lake Constance region. The secondary sector — in particular mechanics ### Salary levels by level of training
In Switzerland, the salary level is closely linked to the training path. The Confederation traditionally distinguishes four levels: compulsory education, secondary education II (apprenticeship or maturity), non-university tertiary education (SFP) and university education ( bachelor's, master's, doctorate). With the same sector, those who have a university degree have access to higher salaries, but the range can vary significantly between sectors.
In the Canton of St. Gallen, aggregate wage data for the entire labour market is published periodically by the UST/BFS, which tracks the structure of wages on a national scale. The Confederation does not set a statutory minimum wage at the federal level: the wage is determined by supply and demand, the CCLs and individual bargaining. However, several cantons — notably Geneva, Neuchâtel, Jura and Basel-City — have introduced a cantonal minimum wage by law. St. Gallen does not fall within these Cantons: therefore, the principle of contractual freedom applies, tempered by the sectoral CCLs where present.
For guidance, it is useful to consider the Swiss median salary as a reference point: the exact figure is updated annually by the UST/BFS and is indexed on a national scale. The coordinated salary for the purposes of the LPP/BVG, on the other hand, depends on the age group of the worker: 7% for those between 25 and 34
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to navigate the job search in St. Gallen
For those looking for a job in the Canton of St. Gallen, the first step is to consult the national job boards and the cantonal placement portals. SECO manages the public employment service and provides information on professions in demand. At the same time, the regional placement offices (RAV/URC) offer support in preparing your application file and in matching supply and demand.
Before signing a contract, it is essential to check some key elements: the salary offered compared to the reference market, the existence of a sector-specific collective labour agreement (CLA/CCL) with any general obligation, the duration of holidays and the notice clauses. Federal law provides for increasing notice periods based on seniority: one month during the first year of service, two months from the second to the ninth year, three months from the tenth year onwards.
### Procedure for those moving to Switzerland
For a Swiss citizen or a permit holder who wishes to work in St. Gallen, the process is relatively straightforward: active search through specialised portals, sending the application file, interview and signing of the contract. For foreign nationals coming from third countries, the issuance of the residence permit (L or B) falls under the responsibility of the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). EU/EFTA citizens benefit from facilitated access to the Swiss labour market thanks to the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons.
Once hired, social security contributions are deducted directly from the payslip: OASI/DI/IC (AVS/AI/IPG), unemployment insurance (AD/AC), accident and occupational illness insurance (LAINF/LAA) and occupational pension (LPP/BVG). The employee enrolled in the LPP contributes according to the age bracket and the coordinated salary, an amount that the employer pays in equal parts. To complete the pension coverage, many workers also take out a 3a pillar, whose annual maximum contribution is indexed by the Confederation.
### Health insurance and cost of living
Every resident in Switzerland is required to take out mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) within three months of arrival or birth. ## In a nutshell - Starting a business in Switzerland requires legal form, capital and registration - The Swiss tax system has three levels: federal, cantonal and municipal - Insurance obligations (AVS, LPP, LAMal) start from the establishment of the company - The cantonal offices manage the registration in the commercial register
## Key facts - **What**: procedure to open a business in the Canton of St. Gallen - When: current administrative procedure - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, Switzerland - Who: future entrepreneur or founder - Amount: minimum capital and registration fees according to the legal form
Those who want to open a business in the Canton of St. Gallen are faced with a defined administrative path: choice of legal form, constitution of capital, registration in the trade register and opening of contributory accounts. Federal Switzerland regulates the types of companies and capital requirements, while the cantons manage the execution of procedures through their trade register offices.
### Main legal forms The sole proprietorship is the simplest form: it does not require minimum capital, but the entrepreneur responds unlimitedly with his own assets. The partnership (simple partnership, partnership, limited partnership) does not have its own legal personality; the shareholders are jointly and severally liable. The limited company — the joint stock company (SA) and the limited warranty company (SAGL) ## Practical analysis: what changes in the entrepreneur's life
Opening a business in St. Gallen is not just an administrative act: it is the start of a series of recurring obligations towards the Confederation, the Canton and the Municipalities. Understanding the structure of these obligations is essential to avoid penalties and properly plan the treasury.
## # Three-tier taxation Switzerland applies a three-tier tax system: the direct federal tax (DFI) is collected by the Confederation through the AFC; cantonal and municipal taxes are regulated by the legislation of the Canton of St. Gallen and by the municipal multiplier. Each Sangallen municipality applies its own multiplier on the basis of the cantonal tax. For an enterprise, this means three coordinated statements but potentially with different deadlines.
### Salary contributions If the activity involves employees, the employer pays AVS/AI/IPG contributions (10.6% total, of which 5.3% is borne by the employee), AD/AC contributions (1.1% up to the annual ceiling) and LAINF/LAA premiums (between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector). For compulsory occupational pension (LPP), the employer's minimum contributions on the coordinated salary are: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55+ up to the reference age). SUVA is the standard insurer for occupational accidents in many industries.
### Founder Health Coverage The founder resident in Switzerland must take out health insurance
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Operational procedure: how to start the business
Starting a business in the Canton of St. Gallen requires a precise sequence of steps. Here is a practical guide based on the information from the source and on general notions of Swiss law.
### Step 1 — Choose the right legal form The decision influences minimum capital, liability, and administrative complexity. The sole proprietorship (ditta individuale) is suited for low-risk activities; the Sagl (GmbH equivalent) balances asset protection and management simplicity; the SA (AG equivalent) is suitable for projects with many investors or plans for going public.
### Step 2 — Draft the articles of incorporation For SA and Sagl, a notarial public deed is required, including the articles of association, subscribed and paid-in capital, and appointment of the governing bodies (board of directors, audit office if mandatory). For a sole proprietorship and partnerships, a notary is not required.
### Step 3 — Deposit the capital The capital must be paid into a bank account in the name of the new company, or covered by documented contributions in kind. The bank issues a payment confirmation required for registration.
### Step 4 — Register with the commercial register The application for registration must be submitted to the Commercial Register Office of the Canton of St. Gallen, together with the required documents and payment of the federal and cantonal registration fees. The source indicates that these fees are regulated; the exact amounts are not specified in the provided text and must be verified with the cantonal office.
### Step 5 — Opening of contribution accounts After registration, the company registers with the AVS compensation fund competent for the area, takes out an accident insurance policy (LAINF/LAA – SUVA/AIA), and, if it has employees, affiliates the workers with the occupational pension scheme (LPP/BVG) through a pension fund.
### Step 6 — VAT registration and permits If turnover exceeds the legal threshold, registration with the AFC/ESTV (Federal Tax Administration) for VAT is required. Some activities require sector-specific authorisations (restaurants, healthcare, construction): enquire with the Canton.
### What to do if capital is limited A potential entrepreneur with limited resources may consider a sole proprietorship or a partnership, which do not require minimum capital. The Sagl remains an option for those who wish to separate personal assets.
### Useful tools To estimate the tax impact of a self-employed activity, it is advisable to use a [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator). For those looking for a current account suited to a new business, the [Swiss banks comparator](nav:banks) helps compare offers. For those who instead want to first assess the cost of living in the Canton of St. Gallen, the [cost of living tool](nav:cost-of-living) provides a realistic overview.
### Indicative timelines From the capital deposit to the effective registration with the commercial register, it usually takes anywhere from a few days to a few weeks, depending on the completeness of the documentation and the workload of the cantonal office. The planning of AVS and LAINF contributions runs from the registration date, not from the date the activity effectively begins.

Incorporation and public deed: for Sagl and SA a public deed before a notary is required; the founding partners sign the articles of association and deposit the capital into a blocked account. 3. Registration with the commercial register of the Canton of St. Gallen: the application is submitted to the cantonal commercial register office, which retains the registration fee according to the cantonal tariff. Opening of a business account and social insurance: opening of a business bank account and registration with the AVS compensation funds, unemployment insurance (AD/AC), SUVA for occupational accidents, and a BVG/LPP pension fund. For amounts that change every year (3rd pillar 3a maximum, LPP coordination threshold, AD/AC maximum, average LAMal premiums, median salary) please refer to the official sources: FSO/BFS for statistics, SECO for the labour market, FSIO/BSV for AVS and LPP, FTA/ESTV for taxes and VAT.

item.title: St. Gallen Transportation Subscriptions: Zones and Rates
item.description: Discover the tariff structure of the Canton of St. Gallen: tariff community, zones, annual and monthly subscriptions, Half-price and AG, discounts for students.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Canton of St. Gallen: transport organized in areas with progressive tariffs - Annual and monthly subscriptions offer discounts compared to single tickets - Half-price and AG combine with local subscriptions for more flexibility - Students and apprentices access dedicated discounts
## Key facts - **What**: Zone-based fare system for regional public transport - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, north-eastern Switzerland - Who: Residents, workers, students, apprentices - Type: Annual, monthly subscriptions, combinable with Half-price and AG - Slat: All regular public transport passengers
The public transport fare system in the Canton of St. Gallen follows the organisational model widespread in Switzerland: a fare community coordinates fares across different geographical areas and ensures the compatibility of subscriptions between different public carriers. This integrated approach represents one of the pillars of Swiss mobility, allowing residents and workers to move on public networks without tariff fragmentation.
### Zone structure: how it works
The zoned structure is the foundation of the Swiss tariff system and the Canton of St. Gallen. Each zone corresponds to a defined geographical area, and the price of the ticket depends on the number of zones crossed. Those who move within a single zone pay less than those who cross several. This logic makes public transport flexible and convenient for short journeys ### Annual and monthly subscriptions: which to choose
The annual subscription in Canton St. Gallen represents the most convenient long-term option for those who plan to use public transport regularly. By paying a single amount, the passenger spreads the cost over twelve months and accesses lower fares compared to the sum of twelve monthly subscriptions purchased individually. This solution is ideal for residents who use public transport daily: commuters who reach their workplace, students attending universities or upper secondary schools in the city, workers with fixed and regular journeys.
The monthly subscription offers greater flexibility instead. Those who do not travel consistently throughout the year, those who know they will change destination in certain months (for example, during school breaks), or those who want to test public transport before committing long-term, find the monthly option most suitable. Monthly prices are higher than one twelfth of the annual cost, but this difference covers and compensates for the advantage of contractual flexibility.
### Half Fare and General Subscription: the national options
The Half Fare is a Swiss national card that reduces by 50% all single tickets and many subscriptions across the entire railway network and most of the Swiss public bus network. In Canton St. Gallen, those who hold a Half Fare card can apply it to the regional subscription, drastically reducing the overall cost. The initial investment in the card pays off quickly for those who travel frequently, making it worthwhile already after a few months of intense use.
The General Subscription (GA) is the most comprehensive solution available in Switzerland: it guarantees unlimited access to trains, buses, trams, and boats across the entire national network. In Canton St. Gallen, a GA holder does not need a separate regional subscription, as the GA already covers local travel. However, those who want a cheaper subscription limited to the canton or a specific geographical area choose a local subscription combined with the Half Fare to obtain significant reductions.
### Combination strategies and evaluation of the choice
The real convenience emerges from the possible combinations between local and national solutions. A passenger could: - Purchase a St. Gallen annual subscription + Half Fare for savings of up to 50% compared to single tickets - Opt for the GA if travel regularly involves all of Switzerland and other regions - Alternate monthly subscriptions during periods of low mobility and annual subscriptions when travel increases (for example, during school months)
The choice depends on the individual mobility profile and travel habits. Those who travel only within the canton and surrounding areas should conveniently choose the local subscription. Those who work in different Swiss cities or travel frequently at a national level for work or study reasons should seriously evaluate the GA option. To compare the different [public transport options](nav:transport) available in your specific area, consult the dedicated tool.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Discounts for students and apprentices
Students and apprentices in the Canton of St. Gallen benefit from dedicated and reduced fares. Middle schools, high schools, and universities often offer discounted school subscriptions at reduced costs, as do vocational training centers and apprenticeship providers. These discounts usually range between 20% and 40% compared to standard fares for the same duration and geographic validity zone.
To access dedicated discounts, official supporting documentation is required: a school card, a letter from the educational institution with a stamp, or an apprenticeship contract. Some carriers require annual renewal of the documentation to maintain the discount, thereby verifying the continuation of the student or apprentice status.
### Procedure to obtain a subscription
1. **Identify your travel zones**: Determine whether you travel within a single zone (single city) or across multiple zones (toward neighboring municipalities, work or study areas). This information is available from the transport operators.
2. Check updated prices: Visit the website of the main transport operator in the Canton of St. Gallen or access the fare lists directly at railway stations and authorized points of sale to compare prices of monthly and annual subscriptions.
3. Evaluate the duration: Analyze your regular travel patterns. If you plan to use public transport almost every day for a year, the annual subscription is economically advantageous. If you are unsure or expect variability, start with monthly subscriptions for 2-3 months to test.
4. Check for any discounts: If you are a student or apprentice, gather the required documentation in advance (school card, institution letter, apprenticeship contract) so you can request the dedicated discounts at the time of purchase.
5. Purchase: Go to authorized points of sale (railway stations, newsstands, carrier ticket offices) or buy online if the carrier offers this option. Keep the purchase documentation and the subscription serial number.
### Mobility and impact on the Swiss budget
Transport subscriptions significantly affect the overall cost of living for every Swiss resident and the monthly household budget. A correct choice of subscription — duration, type of coverage, combinations with Half Fare — can considerably reduce mobility expenses, especially when compared to the costs of a private car (fuel, insurance, maintenance, parking). In the Canton of St. Gallen, where the public network is extensive and well developed, choosing public transport is often the most economical and sustainable solution compared to a personal vehicle.
Consult the [cost of living calculator](nav:cost-of-living) to assess how public mobility fits into your overall Swiss budget and other expense factors (rent, food, energy). With an informed choice of the most suitable subscription for your profile — annual, monthly, with or without Half Fare — you can optimize your mobility budget and significantly reduce the economic impact of your daily commutes in the Canton of St. Gallen.

## Key facts - **What**: Procedure to open a business in Canton Obvaldo - Where: Canton Obvaldo, central Switzerland - Who: Cantonal Authority and Trade Register Office - Taxes: 3 levels (federal + cantonal + municipal DFI) - Minimum capital: To be verified according to the legal form - Social contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee (10.6% total with employer) - Insurance obligation: LAMal mandatory within 3 months of arrival
Starting a business in Canton Obvaldo means moving within a uniform Swiss regulatory framework in substance, but with specific cantonal declinations with regard to taxes, registration fees and administrative charges. The first concrete decision concerns the legal form, because this choice results in minimum capital, accounting obligations, responsibilities and recurring costs.
The main options for those who intend to operate in Obvaldo as an entrepreneur are the sole proprietorship, the joint venture, the limited partnership, Sagl (a limited company) and Sa (a limited company). The first three are not subject to registration in the commercial register, while Sagl and Sa must Choosing the legal form is not just a tax issue: it determines the level of personal responsibility, the ability to raise capital and the accounting obligations. A sole proprietorship is suitable for a low-risk and low-volume business; Sagl and Sa instead offer liability limited to the capital contributed and a structure more suitable for growth and investment.
### Practical implications of salary contributions
Those who start a business and intend to hire staff must consider mandatory social security and insurance contributions in Switzerland. The following apply to the salary paid: AVS/AI/IPG (5.3% borne by the employee, 10.6% total with the employer's share), AD/AC (1.1% up to the annual ceiling provided), LAINF/LAA with rates between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector of activity, and contributions to the second pillar (LPP/BVG) calculated on the salary coordinated according to the age group: 7% (25–34 years), 10% (35–44), 15% (45–54), 18% (55 years up to the reference age). The AVS reference age is currently 65 for men and 64 for women, under harmonisation.
For the owner himself, who is often initially also an employee of his company, the same logic applies: the salary must be consistent with the AVS compensation funds and registered with the compulsory occupational pension fund once the threshold for access to the LPP has been exceeded.
### Insurance and health obligations
Health insurance ### Procedura step-by-step per aprire un'attività in Obvaldo
Passo 1 — Scegliere la forma giuridica. Per attività a basso rischio e con un solo titolare conviene spesso la ditta individuale, che evita l'iscrizione al registro di commercio. Per attività che puntano a crescita, investimenti o responsabilità limitata, Sagl (capitale minimo CHF 20'000) o Sa (CHF 100'000) sono le opzioni standard.
Passo 2 — Verificare la disponibilità della ragione sociale. Prima di costituire la società è opportuno verificare che il nome desiderato non sia già registrato nel registro di commercio svizzero (consultabile online a livello federale).
Passo 3 — Aprire un conto bancario vincolato. Per Sagl e Sa è necessario aprire un conto di deposito del capitale presso una banca svizzera; la banca rilascia una conferma di versamento che andrà allegata alla domanda di iscrizione.
Passo 4 — Redigere l'atto di costituzione e lo statuto. Per Sa e Sagl l'atto costitutivo è un atto pubblico, che in Svizzera richiede la forma autentica davanti a un notaio. Lo statuto disciplina oggetto sociale, capitale, organi e diritti dei soci.
Passo 5 — Iscrivere la società al registro di commercio. La domanda di iscrizione viene presentata all'ufficio cantonale del registro di commercio in Obvaldo, con tutti gli allegati richiesti (atto costitutivo, statuto, conferma bancaria, identità dei fondatori e degli organi).
Passo 6 — Registrarsi presso le autorità fiscali. Dopo l'iscrizione al registro, la nuova entità viene comunicata all'amministrazione cantonale delle contribuzioni, che assegna il numero di contribuente e indica gli obblighi dichiarativi per IFD, imposta cantonale e comunale. Se prevista attività con volume d'affari superiore alla soglia IVA, va effettuata l'iscrizione presso l'AFC/ESTV per l'imposta sul valore aggiunto.
Passo 7 — Iscriversi alle assicurazioni sociali. Il datore di lavoro (anche il titolare che versa uno stipendio a sé stesso) deve affiliarsi a una cassa di compensazione AVS e, se del caso, a una cassa pensioni LPP. La SUVA gestisce l'assicurazione infortuni obbligatoria per i dipendenti; per il titolare indipendente l'adesione è facoltativa ma consigliata.
Passo 8 — Stipulare la LAMal. Il titolare e ogni persona residente in Svizzera deve stipulare un'assicurazione malattia obbligatoria entro tre mesi dall'arrivo o dal trasferimento del domicilio. La scelta della franchigia (CHF 300–2'500 per gli adulti) incide direttamente sul premio mensile.
### Scadenze e adempimenti successivi
Una volta avviata l'attività, vanno rispettate le scadenze periodiche: dichiarazione delle imposte (modulo cantonale e modulo federale), versamenti IVA (di norma trimestrali secondo il metodo concordato con l'AFC), contributi AVS/AI/IPG/AD mensili o trimestrali, premio LAINF e premio LPP. Le quattro date di voto federali all'anno possono occasionalmente riguardare anche temi economici rilevanti per le imprese (riforme fiscali, AVS, LPP); in tali occasioni le conseguenze di un sì o di un no vanno valutate caso per caso.
Per supporto concreto nel calcolo dello stipendio e dei contributi che gravano su dipendenti e datore in Svizzera, è disponibile il [calcolatore stipendio](nav:calculator) di Frontaliere Ticino, utile sia in fase di costituzione sia nella gestione corrente del personale. Per approfondire il confronto dei premi cassa malati tra Cantoni e regioni, è attivo il comparatore casse malati, mentre per la dichiarazione delle imposte e la pianificazione fiscale la [guida dichiarazione imposte](nav:tax-return) offre un quadro operativo aggiornato.

## In a nutshell - Canton of St. Gallen Compensation Fund manages AVS contributions and annuities - Supplementary benefits (PC) cover the minimum living allowance of those entitled - Contribution gaps can reduce the AVS income proportionally - LUFAS/BSV coordinates social security at the federal level
## Key facts - **What**: Cantonal Clearing House of St. Gallen (Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen) - When: Not yet specified in source - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, Switzerland - Who: UFAS/BSV (Confederation) + cantonal clearing houses - Amount: Specific data on annuities and PC thresholds not reported in the source - Legal basis: AVS/AHV managed by the first pillar of Swiss social security - Tools: AVS annuity calculator on the official federal website - Reference: UST/BFS publishes statistics on pensions and PC beneficiaries
Swiss social security is divided into three pillars: the first is the AVS/AHV, which is mandatory for anyone who carries out a gainful activity in Switzerland. In the Canton of St. Gallen, as in all the Cantons, the collection of contributions and the payment of AVS annuities are entrusted to the cantonal compensation fund, which operates under the supervision of the UFAS/BSV at the federal level. The compensation fund is the first point of contact for workers, employers and recipients of annuities.
Registration with the compensation fund generally takes place through the employer, who pays the contributions ## Key facts - **What**: Complementary services (PC) as a safety net of the first pillar - When: Entitlement assessed year by year based on income and substance - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, cantonal PC office - Who: Confederation (UFAS/BSV) + Canton for financing - Amount: Specific amounts and substance thresholds not reported in the source - Procedure: Request at the PC office of the Canton of St. Gallen
When the AVS annuity, possibly added to other benefits of the first and second pillar, is not sufficient to cover the minimum living allowance recognized by law, the supplementary benefits (PC) intervene. It is a benefit subject to conditions of income and substance, financed in part by the Confederation and in part by the Cantons. The UFAS/BSV defines the regulatory framework, while the operational management is entrusted to the cantonal offices of the PCs — also in the Canton of St. Gallen.
### Who is entitled to PCs and how they are calculated
Persons who receive an AVS or AI annuity and whose determining income, net of recognized expenses, does not exceed the recognized expenses for vital needs are potentially entitled to PCs. The expenses recognized include an amount for vital needs (distinguished by single, couple, family), actual rental expenses within a maximum, compulsory health insurance premiums (LAMal/KVG) up to an average cantonal amount, and additional items for particular situations such as
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## Key facts - **What**: Operational procedure for claiming AVS pensions and supplementary benefits - When: Applications at any time, with effect from the date of submission - Where: Compensation fund + PC office of the Canton of St. Gallen - Who: Insured person, employer, cantonal office - Documents: AVS account statement, salary certificates, asset documentation
Obtaining the AVS pension and, if necessary, supplementary benefits is a path that may seem bureaucratic but follows clear steps. Here is how to proceed concretely in the Canton of St. Gallen.
### Step 1: Verify your AVS account
The first step is to request the individual AVS account statement, which lists all recorded earnings and credits for childcare or care tasks. The statement can be obtained online via the federal portal or at the cantonal compensation fund. Any missing income must be reported with supporting documentation (salary certificates, employer attestations).
### Step 2: Apply for the AVS pension
The AVS pension is not paid automatically: it must be formally requested from the compensation fund of the Canton of St. Gallen approximately three to six months before reaching reference age. The application can be submitted online or in paper form and requires personal and bank details as attachments.
### Step 3: Consider redeeming contribution gaps
If the account statement shows contribution gaps in the last five years, a redemption can be considered. However, the redemption is only partly tax-deductible and must be assessed case by case: for people with high incomes, it is often better to leave the gap and compensate through PC; for people with substantial assets, redemption may be more efficient.
### Step 4: Apply for supplementary benefits
If the AVS pension (plus LPP) does not cover the recognised vital needs, a PC application must be submitted to the competent office of the Canton of St. Gallen. Income, asset, rental expense, and LAMal premium documentation are required. The PC is recalculated annually based on the financial situation.
### Step 5: Coordination with other instruments
PC does not exclude other benefits: it cumulates with the reduction of LAMal premiums (cantonal subsidy) and can be supplemented by social assistance benefits for those who still do not reach the minimum subsistence level. It is advisable to also check any entitlement to family supplementary benefits and other cantonal reductions.
To estimate the expected AVS pension amount, the [AVS pension calculator](nav:pension) is useful. To assess the tax impact of a possible redemption, the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) provides an initial indication of net income and applicable deductions in the Canton of St. Gallen.

item.title: AVS and PC in the Canton of St. Gallen: the clearing house
item.description: AVS cashier and PC office are two separate entities: this is how the first pillar works in St. Gallen and when to ask for complementary services.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - AVS first pillar: federal income calculated on a national scale with periodic adjustments - Canton of St. Gallen: the cantonal compensation fund manages AVS contributions and annuities - Complementary services: dedicated cantonal office, separate from the AVS fund - Contribution gaps: extend the contribution period with voluntary payments
## Key facts - **What**: AVS Canton of St. Gallen Compensation Fund and Supplementary Benefits Office - Who: Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen for AVS; Kantonsstelle für Ergänzungsleistungen for PCs - Where: Canton of St. Gallen (German-speaking Switzerland) - When: system in place, operational details updated by cantonal authorities - How it works: cash collects AVS contributions and calculates annuities; PCs are managed by a separate office - Amount: annuity and benefits calculated according to federal legislation AHVG/LPC
In the Canton of St. Gallen, the first pillar of Swiss social security is divided into two distinct bodies that residents must know how to recognize to avoid bureaucratic misunderstandings. The cantonal clearing house — Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen — is the entity that collects the AVS/AI/IPG contributions from workers and employers, calculates the AVS annuities and pays the federal benefits of the first pillar. When an insured reaches the reference age and submits the pension application, it is this fund that verifies the years of contribution, the credits for educational tasks ## Practical analysis: AVS income, gaps and vital minimum
The AVS annuity is not a fixed amount, but the result of a calculation that combines the years of contribution, the average of the income subject to contribution, and credits for educational or assistance tasks. If you are applying for an annuity in the canton of St. Gallen, please contact Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen attaching the individual account statement, salary certificates and any document certifying periods of activity abroad or stay. The cashier then transmits the decision with the indication of the monthly income due.
### What happens in case of contribution gaps Contribution gaps — years in which contributions were not paid, perhaps because the person resided abroad without bilateral agreements or exercised non-subject activity — proportionally reduce the income. The law provides for the possibility of covering them by paying arrears or voluntary contributions, but only under certain terms and conditions. A policyholder who discovers a gap in their individual account can ask the compensation fund for a recovery calculation, knowing that the cost increases with age and that the operation is especially convenient at a young age.

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## What to do concretely: procedure and deadlines
Obtaining the AHV pension or supplementary benefits in the Canton of St. Gallen requires specific steps and adherence to deadlines. The AHV pension application must be submitted to the Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen approximately six months before reaching the reference age. For supplementary benefits, the application is submitted to the Kantonsstelle für Ergänzungsleistungen, attaching the latest AHV pension decision, the LPP pension fund statement, the tax return, and any documentation regarding assets and debts.
### Operational checklist - Request the individual AHV account statement from the Central Compensation Office in Geneva or from the cantonal fund - Verify the completeness of contribution years and identify any gaps - If there are gaps: ask the Ausgleichskasse St. Gallen for a calculation of voluntary or backdated contributions - Submit the AHV pension application approximately six months before the retirement age - Once the AHV decision is received, assess whether the pension covers the minimum subsistence level - If not, submit an application for supplementary benefits (EL) to the Kantonsstelle für Ergänzungsleistungen - Attach all required income and asset documentation
### Useful tools and deadlines EL decisions are recalculated annually: income and assets must be reported every year, failing which payments are suspended. For those already receiving the AHV pension who notice a change in income or family situation (marriage, widowhood, birth of children), it is advisable to submit a new EL application so that eligibility can be reassessed.
To simulate the AHV pension amount and understand the impact of any contribution gaps, the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) is useful, as it allows you to estimate contributions paid over time and the projected pension. To learn more about retirement provision in the Canton of St. Gallen and the mechanisms of the first pillar, the [pension guide](nav:pension) is available, with updated rules on AHV, LPP, and the third pillar.

item.title: Rentals in the Canton of St. Gallen: lease and market rights
item.description: Uniform rental right throughout Switzerland (CO art. 253 et seq.): maximum deposit of 3 months, dispute of the rent within 30 days.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - The CO (art. 253 et seq.) regulates the lease in a uniform manner throughout Switzerland - The security deposit cannot exceed 3 months of rent and goes to a restricted account - The dispute of the initial fee must be submitted within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Cantons and areas affect average canons: St. Gallen is not a single market
## Key facts - **What**: legal framework of the residential lease in the Canton of St. Gallen - When: current federal law (CO art. 253 et seq.), constant application over time - Where: Canton of St. Gallen, with differentiation by areas (urban, peri-urban, rural) - Who: landlord and tenant subject to the Code of Obligations; cantonal conciliation authorities competent for disputes - Amount: maximum security deposit equal to 3 months' rent (not 4, not 6) - Expiry: 30 days to challenge the initial fee before the conciliation authority - Instrument: lease conciliation authority, cantonal body in charge - Principle: same federal lease law in each canton; the variability is on market rents, not on the law
The lease of dwellings and commercial premises is governed by the Code of Obligations (art. 253 et seq.): this is federal law, the same in every Swiss canton. The Canton of St. Gallen has a heterogeneous rental market: urban and peri-urban areas, in particular the city of St. Gallen and neighboring municipalities, show higher rents than rural and mountain areas. The differential is driven by demand (jobs, university, transport supply) and housing availability, not by different cantonal legislation. Those who move to St. Gallen city or a neighboring municipality must therefore take into account higher fees than those who choose an inner valley or a peripheral municipality.
For a potential tenant, there are three critical steps: the verification of the initial rent with respect to the local market, the constitution of the security deposit and the knowledge of their own protection tools in case of disputes. Let's look at them concretely.

## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## What to do concretely in Canton St. Gallen: procedure, deadlines and tools
Renting a home in Canton St. Gallen means facing a precise procedure, with strict deadlines that, if ignored, jeopardize the tenant's rights. Here is an operational guide in four steps.
### Step 1 — Before signing: rent verification
Before signing the lease, compare the proposed rent with: - at least 5–10 similar listings in the same area (same square footage, same type of property, same fittings); - statistical data published by the SFSO (FSO) on the structure of rents in Switzerland; - indications from tenants' associations active in Canton St. Gallen.
If the rent appears abnormal, negotiating before signing is the most effective route. After signing, only ex post tools remain available.
### Step 2 — At signing: security deposit and contract
Verify that the requested deposit does not exceed 3 months' rent. Ask that it be set up in a blocked account held in the tenant's name, at a bank or an insurance company. Keep the payment receipt and all contractual documentation (signed lease, house rules, any ancillary agreements).
Carefully read the clauses on duration, notice periods, rent adjustments and the breakdown of ancillary costs. If anything is unclear, request written clarification before signing.
### Step 3 — Within 30 days: possible rent challenge
If the initial rent is deemed excessive, the tenant may file a challenge with the conciliation authority for tenancy matters of Canton St. Gallen within 30 days of taking possession of the dwelling. The procedure is usually free of charge or low-cost for the parties. The authority first attempts mediation; if it fails, it refers the case to the ordinary court.
### Step 4 — Financial difficulties and affordable rent
If the burden of rent on the household budget becomes critical, it is worth checking whether your municipality or canton provides specific support. At the federal level, tenancy law does not provide direct rent subsidies, but complementary tools exist — including reductions in health insurance premiums (LAMal) for low-income households — that can ease the overall cost of living in Switzerland.
To quickly estimate the impact of rent on your budget and understand how much remains available for other expense items, you can use the Frontaliere Ticino [net salary calculator](nav:calculator). For general information on the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), dedicated guides and comparisons are also available.
